_meta.purpose: EU drone operations (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/947 to Amendment 5, and the operator obligations of Regulation (EU) 2021/664) in CatalogFile shape, so applyCatalogFile creates the framework, its 51 requirements, 53 control templates, their requirement links and the seven subcategory packs together.
_meta.grounding: Requirement codes, titles, sections and summaries are generated from src/data/libraries/eu-uas-ops.yaml, so the library import and this catalogue write identical requirement rows. Every template and all task content is authored in this repo from the regulation's binding text, with figures from EASA's AMC and GM attributed in prose.
_meta.packs: One pack per operating subcategory: A1, A2, A3, STS-01, STS-02, operational authorisation and LUC, each naming the aircraft classes it admits, plus a class C2 pack that installs A2 and A3 together, because a C2 aircraft may fly in either. A pack carries the ten controls every operation needs, the controls common to its category and its own. Install requires choosing at least one; a template the chosen packs share is installed once.
_meta.packApplicability: A pack's controls cite only requirements that govern its subcategory, and cite every one of them. tests/guardrails/eu-uas-framework-coverage.test.ts holds both directions against the table below.

framework.name: EU Drone Operations (Regulation (EU) 2019/947)
framework.description: The operating rules for drones in the EU: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/947 as amended up to Regulation (EU) 2024/1110, which applies from 1 May 2025, together with the U-space operator obligations of Regulation (EU) 2021/664. It is organised by operating subcategory: the open category's A1, A2 and A3, and the specific category's standard scenarios STS-01 and STS-02, operational authorisation and the light UAS operator certificate. Article and point references and titles are the regulation's; the descriptions are Inflect's account of what each asks an operator to demonstrate.

requirements.title: Categories of UAS operations
requirements.summary: Every operation is flown in the 'open', 'specific' or 'certified' category, and the operator can show which and why before it flies. An open operation needs no prior authorisation or declaration; a specific one needs an operational authorisation, a declaration against a standard scenario or an LUC privilege; a certified one needs a certified aircraft and operator.

requirements.title: Rules and procedures for the competency of remote pilots
requirements.summary: Remote pilots hold the competency their category asks for: in the open category the one set in Part A for the subcategory flown, and in the specific category the one the authorisation, standard scenario or LUC sets, covering at least procedures, communication, flight-path and automation management, teamwork, decision-making, situational awareness, workload and handover.

requirements.title: Minimum age for remote pilots
requirements.summary: No remote pilot is younger than 16, except where the regulation allows it (a C0 toy, a privately built aircraft under 250 g, or direct supervision by a pilot who meets the age). A pilot flying under a national derogation that lowers the age does so only on the territory of the State that granted it.

requirements.title: Rules and procedures for the airworthiness of UAS
requirements.summary: Each aircraft meets the technical and airworthiness rules of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/945 for its class, unless it is privately built, flown within a model aircraft club or one of the older aircraft Article 20 still admits, and the operator can show which of those bases applies to every aircraft it flies.

requirements.title: Registration of UAS operators and certified UAS
requirements.summary: The operator is registered in the Member State where it resides or has its principal place of business, and in no other, keeps its registration data accurate, displays its registration number on every aircraft that needs one and loads it into the aircraft's remote identification. A camera or other sensor able to capture personal data makes even a sub-250 g aircraft subject to registration.

requirements.title: Operational conditions for UAS geographical zones
requirements.summary: Before flying, the operator knows the geographical zones each State publishes for safety, security, privacy or environmental reasons, applies the conditions a zone imposes (prohibitions, prior authorisation, class or equipment restrictions) and holds any permission a zone requires.

requirements.title: Safety information
requirements.summary: The operator reports safety-related occurrences to the competent authority as Regulation (EU) No 376/2014 requires, and exchanges safety information about its aircraft. For operations that need no certificate or declaration, the mandatory set is the occurrences that caused a fatal or serious injury or involved an aircraft other than an unmanned one.

requirements.title: Obligations of UAS operators in U-space airspace (Regulation (EU) 2021/664)
requirements.summary: Where a State has designated U-space airspace, the operator flies there only with the mandatory U-space services (network identification, geo-awareness, flight authorisation and traffic information) from a certified service provider, submits a flight authorisation request before each individual flight and complies with the authorisation it receives.

requirements.title: 'Open' category of UAS operations
requirements.summary: An operation stays in the open category only while all of its conditions hold: an eligible aircraft under 25 kg, a safe distance from people and never over assemblies, visual line of sight, no higher than 120 m, and no dangerous goods carried or material dropped. Breaking any one of them makes it a specific-category operation.

requirements.title: Particular provisions concerning the use of certain UAS in the 'open' category
requirements.summary: An aircraft that carries no class label and is not privately built may still fly in the open category only if it was placed on the market before 1 January 2024: in subcategory A1 when it weighs less than 250 g, and in subcategory A3 when it weighs less than 25 kg.

requirements.title: General provisions
requirements.summary: Open-category flights stay within 120 m of the closest point of the earth's surface, measured with the terrain. Near an artificial obstacle taller than 105 m the limit may rise to 15 m above it, but only at the request of the entity responsible for the obstacle.

requirements.title: Responsibilities of the UAS operator
requirements.summary: The operator has procedures suited to the operation and its risk, uses radio spectrum without causing interference, designates a remote pilot for every flight, makes sure pilots and support staff are competent, know its procedures and the manufacturer's instructions and have the zone information, keeps the geo-awareness data current, keeps each class aircraft with its declaration of conformity and class label, and in A2 and A3 has every involved person informed of the risks and consenting.

requirements.title: Responsibilities of the remote pilot
requirements.summary: Before each flight the remote pilot is competent and carries proof of it, has current zone information, has checked the area, obstacles and people, and has an aircraft fit to fly with active remote identification and a payload within its mass limits. In flight the pilot is fit, keeps visual line of sight, respects zone limits, keeps control, follows the operator's procedures and keeps clear of emergency responses.

requirements.title: Duration and validity of the remote pilot online theoretical competency and certificates of remote pilot competency
requirements.summary: The A1/A3 online competency and the A2 certificate each last five years. The operator can show how each pilot revalidates within validity, by demonstrating competencies again or by refresher training from the competent authority or its designated entity, and that a pilot whose credential has expired re-sits the examination.

requirements.title: UAS operations in subcategory A1
requirements.summary: Subcategory A1 flights never overfly assemblies of people. With a class C1 aircraft the pilot expects no uninvolved person to be overflown and keeps any unexpected overflight short; only the lightest aircraft (class C0, privately built or legacy under 250 g) may overfly uninvolved people. A C1 pilot has passed the online training and examination.

requirements.title: UAS operations in subcategory A2
requirements.summary: Subcategory A2 flights use a class C2 aircraft with active and updated remote identification and geo-awareness, never overfly uninvolved people, and keep at least 30 m from them, or 5 m in low-speed mode after the pilot has evaluated the conditions. The pilot holds the A2 certificate of remote pilot competency.

requirements.title: UAS operations in subcategory A3
requirements.summary: Subcategory A3 flights take place where no uninvolved person will be endangered during the whole operation and at least 150 m from residential, commercial, industrial and recreational areas, with an eligible aircraft under 25 kg. The pilot has passed the A1/A3 online training and examination.

requirements.title: 'Specific' category of UAS operations
requirements.summary: An operation that cannot meet the open category's conditions is flown only on a basis the specific category recognises: an operational authorisation from the competent authority of the State of registration, a declaration against a standard scenario, or the privileges of a light UAS operator certificate.

requirements.title: Cross-border operations or operations outside the state of registration
requirements.summary: Before a specific-category operation takes place partly or wholly in another Member State, the operator gives that State's competent authority what it needs: for an authorised operation, a copy of the authorisation and the locations with any updated mitigations, and the operation waits for that authority's confirmation; for a declared operation or an LUC operation, the declaration or terms of approval.

requirements.title: General provisions
requirements.summary: The operator's basis for each specific operation is a risk assessment, a declaration or an LUC with the right privileges, and the operator regularly evaluates whether its mitigations remain adequate and updates them when they are not.

requirements.title: Responsibilities of the UAS operator
requirements.summary: The operator has procedures and limitations for safety, security, protection against unlawful interference, data protection and nuisance; designates a pilot for each flight; trains pilots and essential staff to the competency its basis requires; flies within its declared or authorised limits; keeps personnel, maintenance and operations records for at least three years; maintains its aircraft with qualified staff; and fits every aircraft with a green flashing light and active remote identification.

requirements.title: Responsibilities of the remote pilot
requirements.summary: The remote pilot is fit, competent and carries proof of competency. Before flight the pilot has current zone information, a compatible operating environment, a safe aircraft with active remote identification and has informed the air traffic service and others as required; in flight the pilot stays within the limits, avoids collision with manned aircraft, respects zones and procedures and keeps clear of emergency responses.

requirements.title: Access
requirements.summary: The operator gives any person the competent authority has authorised access to any facility, aircraft, document, record, data or procedure relevant to its declared or authorised activity, including activity it has contracted out.

requirements.title: Use of certified equipment and certified unmanned aircraft
requirements.summary: Where the operator flies a certificated aircraft, it complies with Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1107; where it fits certified equipment to an uncertificated aircraft, it records the equipment's service time, follows its instructions and airworthiness directives and applies mandated safety measures and mandatory safety information.

requirements.title: Operational declaration
requirements.summary: An operator whose operation fits a standard scenario may declare it to the competent authority of its State of registration instead of applying for an authorisation. The declaration states the operation complies with the scenario, commits to its mitigations and confirms insurance where required; the operation starts only once the authority confirms receipt and completeness, and any change is notified without delay.

requirements.title: Duration and validity of an operational declaration
requirements.summary: A declaration lasts two years. It stops counting as complete if the authority finds the operation is not run as declared, if the conditions change so it no longer complies, or if the authority is refused access.

requirements.title: General provisions
requirements.summary: STS-01 flights stay within 120 m of the surface (or 15 m above a tall obstacle at its owner's request), the operational volume reaches no more than 30 m above that limit, and the aircraft carries no dangerous goods.

requirements.title: UAS operations in STS-01
requirements.summary: STS-01 flights are flown in visual line of sight, to the operations manual, over a controlled ground area made up of the flight geography, a contingency area at least 10 m beyond it and a ground risk buffer sized by height and mass, at a ground speed below 5 m/s, by a pilot holding the standard-scenario theoretical certificate and STS-01 practical accreditation, with a class C5 aircraft.

requirements.title: Responsibilities of the UAS operator
requirements.summary: The STS-01 operator writes an operations manual, defines the operational volume and ground risk buffer, proves its contingency and emergency procedures by flight test or simulation, keeps an emergency response plan, checks external services, loads zone data where required, has the controlled ground area in place before each flight, has everyone inside it informed and consenting, and keeps each aircraft's C5 conformity documents and label.

requirements.title: Responsibilities of the remote pilot
requirements.summary: The STS-01 remote pilot checks before each flight that the flight termination means work and remote identification is active, and in flight keeps the aircraft in visual line of sight with a thorough airspace scan, may be assisted by an observer with clear communication, keeps control and discontinues the flight when it poses a risk.

requirements.title: General provisions
requirements.summary: STS-02 flights stay within 120 m of the surface (or 15 m above a tall obstacle at its owner's request), the operational volume reaches no more than 30 m above that limit, and the aircraft carries no dangerous goods.

requirements.title: UAS operations in STS-02
requirements.summary: STS-02 flights are flown to the operations manual over a controlled ground area entirely in a sparsely populated environment, with a ground risk buffer at least the distance the aircraft would likely travel after flight termination, in visibility above 5 km, within 1 km of the pilot without observers or 2 km with them, by an accredited pilot, with a class C6 aircraft that cannot breach its flight geography.

requirements.title: Responsibilities of the UAS operator
requirements.summary: The STS-02 operator writes an operations manual, defines the operational volume and ground risk buffer, proves its contingency and emergency procedures, keeps an emergency response plan, checks external services, loads zone data where required, takes measures against intrusion into the controlled ground area, has everyone inside it informed and consenting, and prepares its airspace observers before the operation.

requirements.title: Responsibilities of the remote pilot
requirements.summary: The STS-02 remote pilot verifies the flight termination means and remote identification before each flight, keeps the aircraft in sight at launch and recovery, flies a pre-programmed trajectory when it is out of sight, and discontinues the flight when it poses a risk.

requirements.title: Responsibilities of the airspace observer
requirements.summary: An airspace observer scans the airspace around the aircraft for manned traffic, keeps track of where the aircraft is, directly or with electronic help, and alerts the remote pilot to any hazard so it can be avoided.

requirements.title: Rules for conducting an operational risk assessment
requirements.summary: The operator's risk assessment describes the operation, sets safety objectives, determines the unmitigated ground and air risk, identifies mitigations (containment, strategic limits, common rules and airspace, adverse conditions, organisational measures) and the robustness each needs. SORA 2.5, the acceptable means of compliance, or a predefined risk assessment are the established ways to do it.

requirements.title: Authorising operations in the 'specific' category
requirements.summary: The competent authority grants an operational authorisation only when the risk assessment's objectives and mitigations are adequate and robust and the operator has confirmed compliance with Union and national rules on privacy, data protection, liability, insurance, security and the environment. The authorisation sets the scope, conditions, mitigations, locations and records the operator must then keep to.

requirements.title: Application for an operational authorisation
requirements.summary: Before an operation the authorisation route requires, the operator applies to the competent authority of its State of registration with its registration number, the accountable manager's name, the risk assessment, the proposed mitigations, an operations manual where the risk and complexity need one and confirmation of insurance where required, and applies again on any significant change.

requirements.title: Issuing of an operational authorisation
requirements.summary: An authorisation is issued once the application is complete and, for any part of the operation in controlled airspace, a procedure for coordination with the airspace service provider is in place; it states its exact scope.

requirements.title: Transferability of an operational authorisation
requirements.summary: An operational authorisation belongs to the operator it was issued to and cannot be transferred to another.

requirements.title: Duration and validity of an operational authorisation
requirements.summary: An operational authorisation lasts as long as it states and only while the operator complies with the regulation and its conditions. When it is revoked or surrendered, the operator returns a digital acknowledgement to the competent authority without delay.

requirements.title: General requirements for an LUC
requirements.section: K. Specific: light UAS operator certificate (LUC)
requirements.category: K. Specific: light UAS operator certificate (LUC)
requirements.summary: Only a legal person may apply for an LUC. The application describes the management system, including the organisational structure and the safety management system, names the responsible personnel including the person who authorises operations, and states that the documents have been verified as compliant.

requirements.title: Responsibilities of the LUC holder
requirements.section: K. Specific: light UAS operator certificate (LUC)
requirements.category: K. Specific: light UAS operator certificate (LUC)
requirements.summary: The LUC holder meets the operator and pilot responsibilities of the specific category, stays within its terms of approval, exercises operational control over every operation under its LUC, risk-assesses each operation that needs it, and keeps risk assessments, mitigations and personnel records for at least three years, protected from damage, alteration and theft.

requirements.title: Safety management system
requirements.section: K. Specific: light UAS operator certificate (LUC)
requirements.category: K. Specific: light UAS operator certificate (LUC)
requirements.summary: The LUC holder runs a safety management system proportionate to its size and activities: an accountable manager, clear responsibilities, a safety policy and objectives, key safety personnel, safety risk management, safety promotion, documented key processes, an independent compliance monitoring function and oversight of what subcontractors deliver.

requirements.title: LUC manual
requirements.section: K. Specific: light UAS operator certificate (LUC)
requirements.category: K. Specific: light UAS operator certificate (LUC)
requirements.summary: The LUC holder gives the competent authority an LUC manual describing its organisation, procedures and activities, with a commitment signed by the accountable manager (and the chief executive when they differ), procedures for partner organisations and subcontractors, amendments sent to the authority and relevant parts distributed to staff.

requirements.title: Terms of approval of the LUC holder
requirements.section: K. Specific: light UAS operator certificate (LUC)
requirements.category: K. Specific: light UAS operator certificate (LUC)
requirements.summary: The LUC is issued once the holder meets the responsibilities, safety management and manual requirements, and it states the operator's identification, privileges, authorised types of operation, authorised area or airspace and any special limitations.

requirements.title: Privileges of the LUC holder
requirements.section: K. Specific: light UAS operator certificate (LUC)
requirements.category: K. Specific: light UAS operator certificate (LUC)
requirements.summary: Within its terms of approval the LUC may grant the holder the privilege to authorise its own operations without submitting a declaration or applying for an operational authorisation; the holder exercises that privilege only as far as the LUC specifies.

requirements.title: Changes in the LUC management system
requirements.section: K. Specific: light UAS operator certificate (LUC)
requirements.category: K. Specific: light UAS operator certificate (LUC)
requirements.summary: A change to the LUC holder's terms of approval, or a significant change to its safety management system, needs the competent authority's approval before it takes effect.

requirements.title: Transferability of an LUC
requirements.section: K. Specific: light UAS operator certificate (LUC)
requirements.category: K. Specific: light UAS operator certificate (LUC)
requirements.summary: An LUC cannot be transferred, except through a change of ownership of the organisation that the competent authority has approved.

requirements.title: Duration and validity of an LUC
requirements.section: K. Specific: light UAS operator certificate (LUC)
requirements.category: K. Specific: light UAS operator certificate (LUC)
requirements.summary: An LUC has no fixed term: it stays valid while the holder complies with the regulation and the issuing State's requirements and has not surrendered it or had it revoked, and on revocation or surrender the holder returns a digital acknowledgement without delay.

requirements.title: Access
requirements.section: K. Specific: light UAS operator certificate (LUC)
requirements.category: K. Specific: light UAS operator certificate (LUC)
requirements.summary: The LUC holder gives any person the competent authority has authorised access to any facility, aircraft, document, record, data or procedure relevant to its certified, authorised or declared activity, including contracted work.

templates.title: Operator registration and registration number on every aircraft
templates.description: The operator is registered once, in the Member State where it resides or has its principal place of business, keeps that registration accurate, displays its registration number on every aircraft that needs it and loads the number into each remote identification system.
templates.objective: To ensure the operator holds one accurate registration in the right Member State and that every aircraft it flies carries and broadcasts that registration number.
templates.successCriteria:
The operator holds one registration, in the Member State of its residence or principal place of business, and in no other State.
The registration record matches the operator's current name, address, contacts, insurance policy and the authorisations, LUC or declarations it holds.
Every aircraft of 250 g or more, or carrying a sensor able to capture personal data, shows the registration number in a form readable on the ground.
Each remote identification system carries the registration number with its secret digits, and the secret digits are known only to named people.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the operator's registration certificate or portal record, with the date of its last update and any expiry the registering State sets.
Obtain the operator's current company or personal details, insurance policy and the list of authorisations, LUC and declarations it holds.
Obtain the fleet register and a dated photograph of the registration number marking on each aircraft in scope.
Obtain the record of who holds the secret digits and the remote identification configuration export or screen capture for each aircraft.

Analysis:
Confirm the registering State is the State of the operator's residence or principal place of business, and search for any second registration.
Compare each field of the registration record with the current details and note any that differ.
Compare the fleet register with the marking photographs and identify any aircraft in scope that carries no readable number.
Compare the operator string in each remote identification system with the registration number and check that access to the secret digits is limited to the named holders.

Output:
A statement of whether the operator is registered once, in the right State, with accurate data.
A list of aircraft in scope that are unmarked, illegibly marked or broadcast a wrong or missing operator string.
Any registration field that is out of date, with the date the change occurred.

title.en: Determine the Member State where the operator must register and confirm no second registration exists

description.en: Article 14(6) requires registration in the Member State of residence for a natural person, or of the principal place of business for a legal person, and forbids holding registrations in two States at once. Decide which State that is, check whether any office, subsidiary or past registration elsewhere has created a second one, and record the decision and its basis.

evidenceHint.en: Signed note naming the registering State and its basis (residence or principal place of business), with the result of the search for other registrations

text.en: Identify the operator's legal residence or principal place of business from company records.
Name the competent authority and registration portal of that Member State.
Ask each office and past operations team whether a registration was ever made in another State.
Cancel any registration found in a second State before relying on the home registration.
Record the registering State, the basis for it and the date the decision was made.

title.en: Register the operator and keep its registration data accurate after every change

description.en: Complete the registration with the fields Article 14(2) lists: identity, address, email and telephone, the insurance policy number where Union or national law requires one, the competence statement a legal person confirms, and the authorisations, LUC or declarations held. The guidance material expects the data to be updated whenever it changes, including when the insurance policy is renewed, so assign an owner and a trigger list.

evidenceHint.en: Registration certificate or portal export showing the operator registration number, current details and the date of the last update

text.en: Enter the operator's identity, address, email and telephone exactly as in company records.
Add the insurance policy number where Union or national law of the registering State requires it.
Confirm the competence statement for legal persons only after the pilot roster shows it is true.
List the operational authorisations, LUC and declarations the operator currently holds.
Name an owner who updates the registration on any change of contact, insurance or authorisation.

title.en: Mark the operator registration number on every aircraft that needs registration

description.en: Article 14(8) requires the registration number on every aircraft meeting the Article 14(5) conditions: in the open category those of 250 g or more, able to transfer more than 80 J on impact, or carrying a sensor able to capture personal data unless they comply with the toy safety directive; in the specific category every aircraft. The AMC expects the number readable on the ground without aids other than corrective lenses, and accepts a QR code or, on small aircraft, a marking in an accessible battery compartment.

evidenceHint.en: Dated photograph of the registration number marking on each aircraft in scope, cross-referenced to the fleet register serial number

text.en: List the aircraft in the fleet register that meet the Article 14(5) registration conditions.
Apply a durable label carrying the operator registration number to each of them.
Check the number can be read on the ground at arm's length without any device.
Photograph each marking and attach the photograph to that aircraft's register entry.
Re-mark the aircraft after any repair, shell replacement or re-painting that removed the label.

title.en: Load the registration number and secret digits into each remote ID and protect the secret digits

description.en: The guidance to Article 14(6) says the operator uploads its registration number and the three secret digits into the remote identification system of each aircraft, and should not share the secret digits with anybody. Load the full string on every aircraft that has remote identification, confirm the system accepts it without an error message, and hold the secret digits as a credential with a short list of named holders.

evidenceHint.en: Per-aircraft record of the remote ID string loaded and accepted, and the access list for the secret digits

text.en: Store the secret digits in the operator's password manager, not in shared documents or emails.
Name the people allowed to read the secret digits and record the list.
Enter the registration number and secret digits through the manufacturer's upload procedure.
Confirm the aircraft accepts the string without the integrity error message the class rules require.
Record the date and the person who loaded the string against each aircraft's register entry.

title.en: Review the operator registration record against current details every year

description.en: Once a year, and whenever the registering State sets a validity period or insurance expiry that is approaching, compare the registration record with the operator's current details and fleet. States may treat a registration as invalid once the recorded insurance expires, and may set a validity period and revoke a number that is not renewed, so check both dates and renew in time.

evidenceHint.en: Annual registration review record listing fields checked, differences found, renewal and insurance expiry dates and corrections made

text.en: Export the current registration record from the registering State's portal.
Compare every field with company records, the insurance certificate and the authorisations held.
Note any registration validity date or insurance expiry the State records and when it falls.
Spot-check the marking and remote ID string of a sample of in-service aircraft.
Correct any difference in the portal and record the review with its date and reviewer.

templates.title: Category and subcategory decided before each operation is planned
templates.description: Before any operation is planned the operator decides, and records, whether it falls in the open category and which subcategory, or in the specific category and on which basis, and refuses work for which it holds no basis.
templates.objective: To ensure every operation is placed in a category and subcategory before planning starts, and that no operation is flown on a basis the operator does not hold.
templates.successCriteria:
Every job record names its category and, for the open category, its subcategory, or for the specific category its basis: STS-01, STS-02, an operational authorisation or the LUC.
Each decision is made before planning, by a named person, against a written trigger list.
Every operation that meets a specific-category trigger is routed to a basis the operator holds, or refused.
No flown operation's track or log contradicts the category recorded for it.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the operator's category decision procedure and its trigger list.
Obtain the job register for the period with the category, subcategory or specific basis recorded for each job and who decided it.
Obtain the operator's current declarations, operational authorisations and LUC terms of approval.
Obtain flight logs and tracks for a sample of jobs.

Analysis:
Check the trigger list covers each open-category condition in Article 4(1): class or privately built aircraft, MTOM under 25 kg, distance from people and no flight over assemblies, VLOS, 120 m, no dangerous goods or dropped material.
Sample jobs and confirm each has a recorded decision dated before planning started.
For each sampled job, compare the logged height, distance, VLOS and payload with the recorded category to find operations flown outside it.
Compare each specific-category job with the declarations, authorisations and LUC held to find jobs with no basis.

Output:
The proportion of sampled jobs with a recorded category decision made before planning.
A list of jobs flown outside the recorded category, or in the specific category without a basis held.
Any gap in the trigger list against the conditions of Article 4(1).

title.en: Write the trigger list that moves an operation out of the open category

description.en: Article 3 places every operation in the open, specific or certified category, and Article 4(1) sets the conditions an open operation must meet. Write a trigger list from those conditions so planners recognise when a job leaves the open category: a flight above 120 m, beyond visual line of sight, over assemblies of people, closer to uninvolved people than the subcategory allows, dangerous goods, dropping material, an MTOM of 25 kg or more, or an aircraft modified outside its class.

evidenceHint.en: Approved category trigger list naming each Article 4(1) condition and the operational situations that breach it

text.en: List each open-category condition from Article 4(1) as a yes or no question for the planner.
Add the subcategory distance and aircraft limits for A1, A2 and A3 that the operator flies.
Add the specific-category triggers the operator meets in practice, such as BVLOS or payload drops.
State that a job needing a certified-category operation is passed to a certified operator.
Approve the list and record its version and approval date.

title.en: Map each operation type to the category basis the operator holds

description.en: List the kinds of work the operator does and, for each, the category and subcategory or specific-category basis it needs. A specific-category basis exists only where the operator has a declaration confirmed under a standard scenario, an operational authorisation, or an LUC with the right privileges. Where an operation type has no basis held, mark it as not offered until one is obtained.

evidenceHint.en: Operation-type matrix showing the category, subcategory or specific basis for each type, with the reference of the declaration, authorisation or LUC held

text.en: List each operation type the operator offers or has flown in the last year.
Assign each type its open subcategory or the specific-category basis it requires.
Record the reference of the confirmed declaration, authorisation or LUC that covers each specific type.
Mark every type with no basis held as not offered and tell the sales and planning teams.

title.en: Record the category decision on each job before flight planning starts

description.en: For every job, the planner runs the trigger list against the site, task and aircraft and records the category and subcategory, or the specific-category basis, with their name and the date. Planning starts only after the decision is recorded, so the distances, competence, aircraft class and paperwork that follow are the ones that category demands.

evidenceHint.en: Job register entries showing category or specific basis, decision maker and decision date ahead of the flight plan date

text.en: Answer each trigger list question for the job's site, task and aircraft.
Record the resulting category and subcategory or specific basis in the job record.
Sign and date the decision before any flight plan is drawn up.
Refuse or reshape the job when it needs a basis the operator does not hold.
Re-run the trigger list if the site, task or aircraft changes after the decision.

title.en: Sample flown jobs each quarter to confirm they stayed in their recorded category

description.en: Each quarter take a sample of completed jobs and compare what was flown with the category recorded for it: height against 120 m, VLOS, distance from people, payload and aircraft used. An operation flown outside its category is a breach of the category rules, not only of the operator's procedure, so record it as a finding and decide whether it is also a reportable occurrence.

evidenceHint.en: Quarterly category sample worksheet listing jobs reviewed, recorded category, flown parameters and findings raised

text.en: Select at least five completed jobs from the quarter across different operation types.
Compare logged height, VLOS, distance to people and payload with the recorded category.
Confirm each job was decided before its flight plan was drawn up.
Raise a finding for any job flown outside its category, with an owner and due date.
Update the trigger list when a sample shows a situation it did not cover.

templates.title: Fleet register with each aircraft's conformity basis
templates.description: The operator keeps one register of every aircraft it flies, stating for each the basis on which it may be operated: its class label, privately built status or pre-2024 legacy status, together with its mass, identification capability and service status.
templates.objective: To ensure the operator knows, for every aircraft it flies, the conformity basis that allows its use and stops any aircraft whose basis has been lost from being flown.
templates.successCriteria:
Every aircraft the operator flies has one register entry with serial number, model, MTOM and conformity basis: class C0 to C6, privately built, or non-class placed on the market before 1 January 2024.
Each entry records the aircraft's remote identification and geo-awareness capability and whether its registration number is marked.
Every aircraft was entered in the register before its first flight for the operator.
An aircraft whose conformity basis is lost is marked quarantined and appears in no flight log after that date.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the fleet register with its change history for the period.
Obtain purchase, delivery and disposal records for aircraft in the period.
Obtain flight logs for the period with the serial number of the aircraft flown.
Obtain declarations of conformity, build records or purchase evidence supporting each aircraft's recorded basis.

Analysis:
Reconcile purchase and disposal records with the register to find aircraft missing from it or still listed after disposal.
For a sample of entries, compare the recorded basis with the declaration of conformity, build record or proof of market placement before 1 January 2024.
Compare the serial numbers in the flight logs with the register to find flights on unregistered aircraft or before the aircraft was entered.
Check that quarantined aircraft do not appear in flight logs after the quarantine date.

Output:
A list of aircraft missing from the register, or listed without a supported conformity basis.
A list of flights made on aircraft not in the register, before entry, or after quarantine.
A statement of whether the register is complete for the period.

title.en: Define the fields of the fleet register and the conformity bases it accepts

description.en: Article 10 requires aircraft to meet the product rules of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/945 unless they are privately built, used under Article 16 or covered by Article 20. Define a register with one row per aircraft and a closed list of conformity bases, so every aircraft is recorded under exactly one of them and nobody records an aircraft as simply 'drone'.

evidenceHint.en: Fleet register template listing its fields and the closed list of conformity bases, with approval date

text.en: Include serial number, manufacturer, model, MTOM including payload and date entered.
Offer only these bases: class C0 to C6, privately built, or non-class placed on market before 2024.
Add fields for remote identification, geo-awareness, registration marking and evidence reference.
Add a status field with in service, quarantined and retired as the only values.
Approve the template and record who maintains the register.

title.en: Record each newly received aircraft in the fleet register before its first flight

description.en: When an aircraft arrives, check its serial number against the delivery note, read its class label or establish that it is privately built or a legacy aircraft placed on the market before 1 January 2024, and record the evidence. Only an aircraft entered as in service may be assigned to a flight.

evidenceHint.en: Fleet register entry with serial number, conformity basis, supporting document reference and entry date earlier than the first flight log

text.en: Match the serial number on the aircraft with the delivery note and invoice.
Record the class label shown on the aircraft, or the privately built or legacy basis and its proof.
Record the MTOM including the heaviest payload the operator will fit.
Record whether the aircraft has remote identification and geo-awareness.
Set the status to in service only after the registration number marking is applied.

title.en: Mark an aircraft quarantined in the fleet register when its conformity basis is lost

description.en: A modification or payload the manufacturer did not foresee, or maintenance outside the manufacturer's instructions, can remove the basis on which an aircraft is flown. When that happens, mark the aircraft quarantined in the register so it cannot be assigned, and record what happened and what would restore it, or the category it may still be used in.

evidenceHint.en: Register entry showing the quarantine date, reason, decision maker and the restoration or re-categorisation decision

text.en: Set the aircraft's status to quarantined on the day the loss of basis is found.
Record the modification, payload or maintenance event that caused it.
Remove the aircraft from any planned flights and tell the affected pilots.
Record the decision to restore, re-categorise or retire the aircraft and who made it.

title.en: Reconcile the fleet register with purchase records and flight logs every quarter

description.en: Each quarter compare the register with purchase and disposal records and with the serial numbers in the flight logs. This finds aircraft flown but never entered, aircraft disposed of but still listed, and quarantined aircraft that were flown anyway.

evidenceHint.en: Quarterly fleet reconciliation record listing discrepancies found between register, purchases, disposals and flight logs, and their resolution

text.en: Export the purchase and disposal records for the quarter.
Export the serial numbers of every aircraft that appears in the quarter's flight logs.
List aircraft flown that are missing from the register or were flown before their entry date.
List quarantined or retired aircraft that appear in a flight log after their status date.
Raise a finding for each discrepancy and record how it was resolved.

templates.title: Remote pilot roster with credentials, expiry and age
templates.description: The operator keeps a roster of its remote pilots stating each credential they hold, its identification number, issuing State and expiry, verifies each pilot's age, and assigns a pilot only to work their credentials cover.
templates.objective: To ensure every remote pilot the operator assigns meets the minimum age and holds a current credential for the category and subcategory of the work they fly.
templates.successCriteria:
Every remote pilot who flies for the operator is on the roster with each credential held, its identification number, issuing authority, issue date and expiry date.
Each pilot's age was verified at onboarding against the minimum of 16 years or a national derogation, recorded with the territory it is valid in.
No flight log shows a pilot flying a subcategory or scenario for which the roster held no current credential on that date.
Pilots are alerted to credential expiry at least three months ahead.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the pilot roster with its change history for the period.
Obtain copies of each pilot's proofs of competency and the record of age verification.
Obtain flight logs for the period showing the pilot and the category or subcategory flown.
Obtain any national derogation on minimum age the operator relies on.

Analysis:
Compare each roster entry with the proof of competency it cites, checking the identification number, issuer and dates.
Confirm each pilot's recorded date of birth gives at least 16 years at onboarding, or that a national derogation applies and the pilot flies only in that State.
Sample flight logs and check that on each date the pilot held a current credential for the subcategory, scenario or authorisation flown.
Check that expiry alerts were issued ahead of each expiry in the period.

Output:
A list of roster entries not supported by a proof of competency or carrying wrong dates.
A list of flights made by a pilot without a current credential for that work.
Any pilot under 16 without a valid derogation, or flying outside the derogating State.

title.en: Define the credentials each subcategory, scenario and authorisation requires of a remote pilot

description.en: Article 8 sets competency through Part A of the Annex for the open category and through the operational authorisation, standard scenario or LUC for the specific category. Write down, for each kind of work the operator does, which credential a pilot must hold, so the roster and the rostering rule can be checked against one list.

evidenceHint.en: Credential requirements table mapping each subcategory, scenario or authorisation to the pilot credential it needs

text.en: List each open subcategory and specific-category basis the operator flies under.
Name the credential each one requires, such as the A1/A3 proof, the A2 certificate or STS certificate.
Add any training an operational authorisation or the LUC terms specify for its pilots.
Approve the table and record its version and date.

title.en: Verify each new remote pilot's age against Article 9 at onboarding

description.en: Article 9 sets a minimum age of 16 for remote pilots in the open and specific categories. A Member State may lower it by up to four years in the open category or two in the specific category, but only for flights on its own territory, and direct supervision by a pilot meeting the age rule is also allowed. Check identity documents and record the result.

evidenceHint.en: Onboarding record showing identity document checked, date of birth, age verdict and any national derogation with the territory it is valid in

text.en: Check the pilot's identity document and record the date of birth.
Confirm the pilot is at least 16 on the onboarding date.
For a younger pilot, record the national derogation relied on and limit them to that State.
Record any supervision arrangement and the supervising pilot's name.

title.en: Record every pilot credential in the roster with its number, issuer and expiry

description.en: Enter each pilot's credentials in the roster from the proofs themselves. The AMC gives remote pilot identification numbers the form NNN-RP-xxxxxxxxxxxx, where NNN is the issuing State's three-letter code, which lets an entry be traced to its issuer. Attach a copy of each proof.

evidenceHint.en: Roster entries with credential type, identification number, issuing authority, issue and expiry dates, and an attached copy of each proof

text.en: Copy the credential type and identification number exactly from the proof.
Record the issuing competent authority or designated entity and its State.
Record the issue date and the expiry date printed on the proof.
Attach a scan of the proof and set an expiry alert three and six months ahead.

title.en: Check the roster before assigning a remote pilot to any flight

description.en: Before a pilot is assigned, the planner checks the roster for a current credential that matches the job's recorded category, subcategory or specific basis. A pilot whose credential has expired, or who holds none for that work, is not assigned, however experienced they are.

evidenceHint.en: Flight assignment records showing the roster check, the credential relied on and its expiry date for each assigned pilot

text.en: Read the job's recorded category and subcategory or specific basis.
Look up the pilot's current credentials in the roster.
Confirm the credential covers the job and is valid on every flight date.
Record the credential relied on in the flight assignment.
Assign a different pilot when the check fails, and record why.

title.en: Reconcile the pilot roster with the quarter's flight logs and expiring credentials

description.en: Each quarter compare who flew, what they flew and on which date with what the roster held on that date, and list every credential due to expire in the next six months. This finds pilots who flew without cover and expiries nobody has started to deal with.

evidenceHint.en: Quarterly roster reconciliation listing flights checked, uncovered flights found and credentials expiring in the next six months with their owners

text.en: Export the quarter's flights with pilot, date and recorded category.
Match each flight to the credential the roster held for that pilot on that date.
Raise a finding for each flight made without a current credential for the work.
List credentials expiring in the next six months and confirm each pilot has been told.

templates.title: Geographical zone information, conditions and permissions
templates.description: For every State it flies in, the operator keeps the official source of geographical zone information, checks each planned area against the zones and their conditions, and obtains any permission a zone requires before flying.
templates.objective: To ensure no operation is flown in a geographical zone without meeting the conditions, limits and prior permissions the Member State set for that zone.
templates.successCriteria:
For each State of operation the operator names the official source of geographical zone data and how temporary zones are published.
Every job record shows a zone check against current data, made before flight, naming the zones affecting the area.
Where a zone requires a prior authorisation, the permission is on file before the flight date and its conditions are reflected in the plan.
No flight log shows an operation inside a zone in breach of its height limit, timing or other conditions.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the operator's list of geographical zone data sources per State of operation.
Obtain the zone checks recorded on job records for the period, with the data version or date used.
Obtain the permissions obtained from zone managers and the zone conditions they impose.
Obtain flight logs and tracks for jobs flown in or near geographical zones.

Analysis:
Check that each listed source is the one the State publishes, such as the source the AIP ENR 5.3.1 section points to.
Sample job records and confirm the zone check was made before flight, against data current at the time.
For sampled jobs in zones requiring prior authorisation, compare the permission date and conditions with the flight date and plan.
Compare tracks with zone boundaries and limits to find flights inside a zone in breach of its conditions.

Output:
A list of States flown in with no named or a wrong zone data source.
A list of jobs without a prior zone check, or flown in a zone without the required permission.
Any flight that breached a zone limit or condition, with the zone and the action taken.

title.en: Identify the official geographical zone data source for each State of operation

description.en: Article 15(3) requires each Member State to publish its zones, with their period of validity, in a common digital format; the AMC names EUROCAE ED-269 for that format and points to the AIP section ENR 5.3.1 for where the data is published, with NOTAMs used for temporary zones. Record, for each State the operator flies in, where the data is and how temporary changes are announced.

evidenceHint.en: Per-State list of official zone data sources, national apps and NOTAM channels, with the date each was last confirmed

text.en: List each Member State the operator flies in or plans to fly in.
Record each State's official zone data source and national map or app.
Record where temporary zones are announced, such as NOTAMs.
Confirm each source against the State's AIP or competent authority website.
Date the list and name who keeps it current.

title.en: Check each planned operating area against current geographical zones before flight

description.en: Under Article 15(1) a zone may prohibit operations, set conditions, require a prior flight authorisation, admit only certain classes or require remote identification or geo-awareness. For every job, check the area and the date against current zone data and NOTAMs, and record which zones apply and what each requires of the flight.

evidenceHint.en: Job record zone check naming the data source and version, the zones affecting the area and the conditions each imposes

text.en: Draw the operating area and planned height on the official zone map for the State.
Check NOTAMs and temporary zones for the planned dates.
Record each zone affecting the area and what it prohibits, limits or requires.
Record the data source and version or download date used for the check.
Stop planning when a zone prohibits the operation and no exemption applies.

title.en: Obtain and file the permission a geographical zone requires before the flight

description.en: Where a zone requires a prior flight authorisation or permission from the entity that manages it, apply in time, file the answer with the job and carry its conditions into the flight plan and briefing. A permission that has not arrived by the flight date means the flight does not go ahead in that zone.

evidenceHint.en: Zone permission or authorisation filed with the job, showing issuer, date, validity and conditions, and the flight plan reflecting them

text.en: Identify the zone manager and the application route the zone data names.
Apply with the area, heights, dates and aircraft the job will use.
File the permission with the job and copy its conditions into the flight plan.
Brief the pilot on the permission's conditions before departure.
Cancel the flight in that zone when no permission is held on the flight date.

title.en: Brief pilots and support staff on the zone conditions for each job

description.en: The operator must give remote pilots and support personnel the geographical zone information relevant to each operation. Include the zones, their limits and any permission conditions in the job briefing, so the people on site know a lower height limit or a time window, not only the planner.

evidenceHint.en: Job briefing record listing the zones and conditions given to the pilot and support staff, with their acknowledgement

text.en: Add a geographical zones section to the job briefing template.
List each zone, its limits and any permission conditions for the job.
Give the briefing to the pilot and every support person before the flight.
Record each person's acknowledgement of the zone briefing.

title.en: Compare a sample of flight tracks with geographical zone limits each month

description.en: Each month take a sample of flights in or near geographical zones and compare the tracks with the zone boundaries, height limits, time windows and permission conditions in force on the flight date. Record each breach as a finding and consider whether it is a reportable occurrence.

evidenceHint.en: Monthly zone compliance sample listing flights reviewed, zones and limits checked, breaches found and findings raised

text.en: Select flights from the month that took place in or within 1 km of a geographical zone.
Overlay each track on the zone data in force on the flight date.
Check heights, times and permission conditions against the track and log.
Raise a finding for each breach with an owner and a due date.
Refresh the zone source list when a sample shows data the operator did not have.

templates.title: U-space airspace services and flight authorisation requests
templates.description: Where a Member State has designated U-space airspace over an operating area, the operator flies there only with the capabilities Regulation (EU) 2021/664 requires, through a U-space service provider, and with a flight authorisation for each flight.
templates.objective: To ensure every flight in designated U-space airspace uses the mandatory U-space services and starts only after its flight authorisation request has been granted.
templates.successCriteria:
The operator holds a current record of which of its operating areas lie in designated U-space airspace, checked at least each quarter.
For any area in U-space airspace, the operator has a contract with a U-space service provider and aircraft meeting the capability requirements.
Every flight in U-space airspace has a flight authorisation request submitted before the flight and an authorisation on record.
No flight in U-space airspace was flown without network identification or outside its authorisation.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the operator's record of U-space airspace designations affecting its operating areas, with the date of each check.
Obtain any contract with a U-space service provider and the provider's certificate.
Obtain flight authorisation requests and grants for flights in U-space airspace in the period.
Obtain flight logs for those flights and the provider's records of network identification.

Analysis:
Compare the operator's areas with the U-space airspace designations published by each State of operation.
For areas inside U-space airspace, confirm a contract exists and that the aircraft used meet the capability requirements the airspace sets.
Match each flight in U-space airspace with a request submitted before the flight and an authorisation granted for it.
Compare flight logs with authorisations and network identification records to find flights outside their authorisation or without identification.

Output:
A statement of which operating areas lie in U-space airspace and whether the record is current.
A list of flights in U-space airspace without a prior authorisation or network identification.
Any gap in provider contracts or aircraft capability for those areas.

title.en: Check whether any operating area lies in designated U-space airspace

description.en: Regulation (EU) 2021/664 applies only inside geographical zones a Member State has designated as U-space airspace, and has applied since 26 January 2023. Check each State's designations against the operator's operating areas. Where none apply, record that, because the answer changes as States designate new airspace.

evidenceHint.en: Dated U-space applicability record listing each operating area, the State's designations checked and the result

text.en: List the operator's regular operating areas by State.
Check each State's published U-space airspace designations.
Mark each area as inside or outside designated U-space airspace.
Record the result with the date and the sources checked.

title.en: Obtain a contract with a certified U-space service provider for areas in U-space airspace

description.en: In U-space airspace operations are subject to four mandatory services: network identification, geo-awareness, UAS flight authorisation and traffic information. The operator uses them through a certified U-space service provider and must meet the capability requirements set for the airspace. Before the first flight there, put a provider contract in place and confirm the aircraft can meet those requirements.

evidenceHint.en: Signed contract with a certified U-space service provider and a record that each aircraft used meets the airspace capability requirements

text.en: Identify the certified U-space service providers for the designated airspace.
Confirm the provider offers all four mandatory services for that airspace.
Sign a service contract and file the provider's certificate with it.
Check each aircraft to be used against the airspace's UAS capability requirements.
Train pilots on the provider's tools before their first flight in the airspace.

title.en: Send a U-space flight authorisation request before each flight in U-space airspace

description.en: Article 6(4) of Regulation (EU) 2021/664 requires a UAS flight authorisation request to the U-space service provider before each individual flight. The pilot flies only once the authorisation is granted, keeps network identification active, and complies with the authorisation and any airspace constraints.

evidenceHint.en: U-space flight authorisation request and grant for each flight, matched to the flight log entry

text.en: Submit the flight authorisation request to the provider before the flight.
Wait for the authorisation and read its conditions before take-off.
Confirm network identification is active through the provider before take-off.
Fly within the authorisation and record its reference in the flight log.

title.en: Reconcile U-space flight authorisations with flight logs each quarter

description.en: Each quarter match every flight logged in U-space airspace with its authorisation and the provider's network identification record, and repeat the designation check for all operating areas. A flight without an authorisation granted before it is a breach to record and act on.

evidenceHint.en: Quarterly U-space reconciliation listing flights matched to authorisations, unmatched flights and the refreshed designation check

text.en: Export the quarter's flights logged in U-space airspace.
Match each flight with an authorisation granted before its take-off time.
Check the provider's identification records for each flight.
Raise a finding for each unmatched flight or identification gap.
Repeat the U-space designation check for every operating area.

templates.title: Occurrence reporting and follow-up
templates.description: The operator records every occurrence internally, reports safety-related occurrences to the competent authority as Article 19 and Regulation (EU) No 376/2014 require, and analyses each one so the cause is addressed.
templates.objective: To ensure every safety-related occurrence is recorded, reported to the competent authority where required within the time allowed, and analysed so its cause is addressed.
templates.successCriteria:
Every occurrence, including near misses, fly-aways, lost links and battery failures, appears in the internal occurrence log with date, aircraft, pilot and description.
Each logged occurrence carries a decision on whether it must be reported to the competent authority, with the reason.
Each report to the competent authority was made no later than 72 hours after the operator became aware of the occurrence.
Each occurrence has an analysis, an action and an owner, and closed actions are verified.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the operator's occurrence reporting procedure and internal occurrence log for the period.
Obtain the reports sent to the competent authority, with submission dates.
Obtain flight logs, maintenance records and incident correspondence for the period.
Obtain the analysis and action records for each occurrence, with the evidence of each closed action.

Analysis:
Search flight logs, maintenance records and correspondence for events that should appear in the occurrence log and do not.
For each logged occurrence, check the reportability decision against the procedure, including the scope that applies to the open category.
Compare each report's submission date with the date the operator became aware of the occurrence.
Check that each occurrence has an analysis and an action, and that closed actions were verified.

Output:
A list of events missing from the occurrence log.
A list of reportable occurrences reported late or not reported.
A list of occurrences without analysis or with actions overdue.

title.en: Define which UAS occurrences the operator must report and which it reports voluntarily

description.en: Article 19(2) requires the operator to report safety-related occurrences under Regulation (EU) No 376/2014. The guidance to Article 19 says that for aircraft needing no certificate or declaration, which is the open category, the mandatory scope is limited to events causing fatal or serious injury or involving an aircraft other than an unmanned one. Specific operations may add reportable events in their authorisation. Write this into the procedure.

evidenceHint.en: Occurrence reporting procedure listing mandatory and voluntary occurrence types per category, the reporting channel and the time limit

text.en: List the mandatory occurrence types for open-category operations from the guidance to Article 19.
Add any extra reportable events listed in the operator's operational authorisations.
List the events the operator reports voluntarily, such as fly-aways and lost links.
Name the competent authority's reporting channel for each State of registration.
State the time limit for reporting and who submits reports.

title.en: Record every occurrence in the internal occurrence log the day it happens

description.en: Every person in the operation logs occurrences, not only the ones that look reportable: near misses with manned aircraft, fly-aways, lost command and control links, remote identification or geo-awareness failures, battery failures, injuries and damage. The log is the population the reporting decision and the analysis work from, so an event missing from it is missing from both.

evidenceHint.en: Internal occurrence log entries with date, time, aircraft serial number, pilot, description and the person who logged it

text.en: Log the occurrence the same day with date, time, location, aircraft and pilot.
Describe what happened and what the pilot did, in plain words.
Attach the flight log, telemetry and photographs available.
Mark the aircraft unserviceable when the occurrence may have damaged it.

title.en: Report each mandatory occurrence to the competent authority within 72 hours

description.en: Regulation (EU) No 376/2014 requires an organisation to report an occurrence to its competent authority as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours after becoming aware of it. For each logged occurrence decide reportability against the procedure, submit through the authority's channel when required, and file the submission receipt with the log entry.

evidenceHint.en: Occurrence log entry showing the reportability decision, and the submission receipt with its timestamp for each reported occurrence

text.en: Decide whether the logged occurrence is reportable and record the reason.
Submit a reportable occurrence through the competent authority's channel.
Confirm the submission was made within 72 hours of becoming aware.
File the submission receipt and reference with the log entry.
Send any follow-up information the authority asks for and record it.

title.en: Analyse each logged occurrence and assign an action to address its cause

description.en: For each occurrence, establish what caused it, whether it could recur and what change would prevent it: a procedure, training, maintenance, a configuration setting or an aircraft withdrawn. Assign each action an owner and a due date, and verify it once done.

evidenceHint.en: Occurrence analysis record with cause, action, owner, due date and verification of the closed action

text.en: Review the evidence attached to the occurrence with the pilot involved.
Record the cause and the conditions that let it happen.
Choose an action that addresses the cause and assign an owner and due date.
Verify the action is in place before closing the occurrence.
Share the lesson with all pilots in a short written notice.

title.en: Review the occurrence log for completeness and late reports each quarter

description.en: Each quarter search flight logs, maintenance records and correspondence for events that never reached the occurrence log, check every reported occurrence against the 72-hour limit, and list open actions. Look for repeated causes across occurrences, which a single analysis does not show.

evidenceHint.en: Quarterly occurrence review listing missing events found, late reports, overdue actions and recurring causes

text.en: Search the quarter's flight and maintenance records for unlogged events.
Check each reported occurrence's submission time against the time of awareness.
List actions past their due date with their owners.
Group occurrences by cause and note any cause that occurred more than once.
Raise a finding for each gap and present the review to the accountable manager.

templates.title: National requirements and insurance for each State of operation
templates.description: The operator keeps a matrix of the national requirements of each State it flies in, including insurance, extra registration data, minimum-age derogations and zone rules, checks each deployment against it, and watches for changes to EU and national rules.
templates.objective: To ensure every operation meets the national requirements of the State it takes place in, including insurance, and that changes to EU or national rules reach the operator before they apply.
templates.successCriteria:
The matrix has one row per State of operation, covering insurance, extra registration identity data, minimum-age derogations, zone rules and penalties, each with a source and review date.
Every deployment to a State has a recorded check against that State's row before the first flight there.
Where a State requires third-party insurance, a current certificate covering the aircraft and operations is held and carried as the State requires.
A regulatory watch is recorded each quarter, with any change assessed and assigned.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the national requirements matrix with its sources and review dates.
Obtain the deployment records for the period with the pre-deployment check for each State.
Obtain the insurance certificates in force during the period and their scope.
Obtain the quarterly regulatory watch records and the follow-up actions they raised.

Analysis:
Compare the States in the matrix with the States in which the operator flew during the period.
For a sample of rows, check the insurance and registration entries against the State's own published rules.
For each sampled deployment, confirm the check was made before the first flight and that the insurance in force covered the aircraft, mass and type of operation.
Check that each quarter has a watch record and that each change found was assessed and assigned.

Output:
A list of States flown in that have no matrix row or a row out of date.
A list of deployments without a prior check or without the insurance the State requires.
Any regulatory change found and not acted on.

title.en: Build the national requirements matrix for every State the operator flies in

description.en: Regulation (EU) 2019/947 itself imposes no insurance duty. Regulation (EC) No 785/2004 applies from 20 kg, and most States require third-party cover for lighter aircraft through national law, as Spain does for A2 operations under Royal Decree 517/2024. Article 14(9) also lets States collect extra registration identity data, and Article 9(3) lets them lower the minimum age. Write one row per State with each requirement and its source.

evidenceHint.en: National requirements matrix with one row per State covering insurance, registration extras, age derogation, zone rules and penalties, each sourced and dated

text.en: List every State the operator flies in or plans to fly in.
Record each State's insurance rule, minimum cover and whether proof must be carried.
Record any extra registration identity data and any national identification marking required.
Record any minimum-age derogation, its territory and the penalty regime.
Cite the official source for each entry and date the row.

title.en: Obtain the insurance each State of operation requires and track the policy expiry

description.en: Arrange third-party liability insurance that meets the strictest requirement of the States in the matrix for the aircraft masses and operations flown. Record the policy in the registration where Union or national law requires the number, track its expiry so it never lapses during operations, and carry proof on flights where a State requires it.

evidenceHint.en: Current insurance certificate with its scope, limits and expiry, mapped to each State's requirement in the matrix

text.en: Compare the policy's cover, limits and territorial scope with each State's row in the matrix.
Confirm the policy covers every aircraft and type of operation in the fleet register.
Set alerts 60 and 30 days before the policy expiry date.
Give pilots a copy of the certificate for flights in States that require it on board.

title.en: Check each deployment against the destination State's row before the first flight

description.en: Registration happens in the home State, but insurance, zone rules and other national conditions follow the State of operation. Before the first flight of any deployment, check the destination State's row in the matrix and confirm each requirement is met: insurance, identification marking, pilot age, zone sources and any notification.

evidenceHint.en: Pre-deployment checklist for the destination State, signed before the first flight, showing each matrix requirement and how it is met

text.en: Open the destination State's row in the national requirements matrix.
Confirm the insurance in force meets that State's requirement.
Confirm any national marking, identity data or notification the State requires is in place.
Confirm the pilots meet the State's age rule and hold credentials it recognises.
Sign and date the checklist before the first flight in that State.

title.en: Run the quarterly watch of EU and national drone rule changes

description.en: Each quarter check for changes that would alter the operator's obligations: the Commission's adoption of the draft rules in EASA Opinion 06/2026, which proposes operator identity verification before registration and lower registration and direct remote identification thresholds; new EASA decisions amending the acceptable means of compliance; and national changes to insurance or zone conditions. Assess each change and assign the work it needs.

evidenceHint.en: Quarterly regulatory watch record listing sources checked, changes found, their effect on the operator and the owner of each follow-up

text.en: Check the Official Journal and EASA for new or adopted UAS acts and decisions.
Check the status of the drafts attached to EASA Opinion 06/2026.
Check each matrix State's competent authority for national changes.
Record each change, its application date and its effect on the operator.
Assign an owner to every change that needs work and update the matrix.

templates.title: Personal data captured by aircraft sensors
templates.description: Imagery, video and other data that identify people, captured by the operator's aircraft sensors, are processed for a stated purpose on a lawful basis, recorded, assessed where required, kept no longer than needed and protected.
templates.objective: To ensure personal data captured by aircraft sensors is processed lawfully for stated purposes, assessed where required, protected, and deleted when no longer needed.
templates.successCriteria:
Each mission type that captures personal data has a stated purpose, a lawful basis and an entry in the record of processing.
A documented decision on the need for a data protection impact assessment exists for each such mission type, and an assessment exists where one is required.
Captured footage has a retention period per mission type and is deleted when it expires.
People likely to be filmed are informed, and access to stored footage is limited to named roles.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the record of processing entries for sensor data and the list of mission types that capture personal data.
Obtain data protection impact assessments and the screening decisions for each mission type.
Obtain the retention schedule for footage and the deletion logs for the period.
Obtain the information notices, signage or briefing material used on site, and the access list for footage storage.

Analysis:
Compare the operator's mission types with the record of processing to find mission types capturing personal data without an entry.
Check each screening decision against the criteria the data protection authority applies, such as systematic monitoring of public spaces.
Sample stored footage and compare its capture dates with the retention period for its mission type.
Compare the access list with the people who actually accessed footage in the period, and check that information was given on sampled jobs.

Output:
A list of mission types with no purpose, lawful basis or processing record.
A list of mission types needing an impact assessment that have none.
Footage held past its retention period, and access by people not on the access list.

title.en: Identify the mission types whose aircraft sensors capture personal data

description.en: Article 14(5) brings an aircraft carrying a sensor able to capture personal data into registration even below 250 g, because such sensors create a privacy risk. The General Data Protection Regulation applies directly to the imagery and telemetry that identify people. List each mission type, the sensors it uses and whether people, number plates or private property are likely to be captured.

evidenceHint.en: Mission type inventory listing sensors used and the personal data each mission type is likely to capture

text.en: List each mission type the operator flies and the sensors fitted for it.
Record whether people, faces, number plates or private gardens are likely to be captured.
Record whether footage is stored, streamed live or sent to a client.
Mark each mission type that processes personal data for the record of processing.

title.en: Record purpose, lawful basis and retention for each sensor-data mission type
