description.en: For each mission type that captures personal data, state its purpose in specific terms rather than a general word such as safety, choose the lawful basis, set how long footage is kept and who receives it, and add an entry to the record of processing. Where the operator flies on a client's instructions, record which party is controller and which processor.

evidenceHint.en: Record of processing entries for each sensor-data mission type with purpose, lawful basis, recipients, retention and controller or processor role

text.en: Write a specific purpose for each mission type in one sentence.
Choose and record the lawful basis for that purpose.
Set a retention period and record who receives the footage.
Record the operator's role as controller or processor and the client's role.
Add the entry to the record of processing with the approval date.

title.en: Assess each sensor-data mission type for the need for a data protection impact assessment

description.en: Decide for each mission type whether processing is likely to result in a high risk and so needs an impact assessment, for example systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area or processing on a large scale. Record the decision and its reasons, and carry out the assessment before the mission type is flown where it is required.

evidenceHint.en: Screening decision per mission type with its reasons, and the completed impact assessment where one is required

text.en: Apply the data protection authority's high-risk criteria to each mission type.
Record whether an impact assessment is required and why.
Carry out the assessment before first flight where it is required.
Record the measures the assessment adopts, such as blurring or reduced resolution.

title.en: Notify people on site and restrict access to stored aircraft footage

description.en: On each job that captures personal data, inform people likely to be filmed through signs, a briefing or a published notice, in line with the transparency rules. Store footage where access is limited to named roles, take particular care with footage of people involved in an emergency, and delete it at the end of its retention period.

evidenceHint.en: Job record showing how people were informed, the footage access list and the deletion log for expired footage

text.en: Put up signs or brief people on site before filming starts.
Upload footage only to the storage location set for the mission type.
Limit access to the roles on the access list and remove leavers promptly.
Delete footage at the end of its retention period and log the deletion.

title.en: Review sensor-data processing, retention and access each year

description.en: Once a year compare the mission types flown with the record of processing, check that impact assessment decisions still hold, sample stored footage for items kept past their retention period, and compare actual access to footage with the access list. Update entries where missions, sensors or clients have changed.

evidenceHint.en: Annual sensor-data review record listing mission types checked, footage sampled, retention breaches, access exceptions and updates made

text.en: Compare the year's mission types with the record of processing entries.
Revisit each impact assessment decision for changed sensors or locations.
Sample stored footage and list any item held past its retention period.
Compare storage access logs with the access list and record exceptions.
Update the entries and assign an owner to each exception found.

templates.title: Maintenance, firmware and payload configuration to the manufacturer's instructions
templates.description: Each aircraft is maintained to its manufacturer's instructions with original or listed parts and allowed payloads only, its software is kept at the version the manufacturer publishes, and any change that would break its conformity is caught before flight.
templates.objective: To ensure every aircraft stays in the condition and configuration its conformity basis assumes, through maintenance, parts, payloads and software kept to the manufacturer's instructions.
templates.successCriteria:
Every aircraft has a maintenance record showing work done to the manufacturer's instructions at the intervals they set.
Every replaced part is original or on the manufacturer's list of replaceable parts, and every payload fitted is one the manufacturer allows, within MTOM.
Aircraft and remote-station software is at the latest version the manufacturer has published before each operating day.
After each software update or repair, remote identification and geo-awareness were re-checked and the result recorded.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the manufacturer's maintenance instructions, list of replaceable parts and allowed payloads for each aircraft model.
Obtain maintenance records, parts purchase records and payload records for the period.
Obtain the software version records for each aircraft and remote station and the manufacturer's release notes.
Obtain the post-update and post-repair check records.

Analysis:
Compare each aircraft's maintenance record with the intervals and tasks in the manufacturer's instructions.
Compare parts fitted with the manufacturer's list of replaceable parts and payloads fitted with the allowed payloads, including mass.
Compare the software versions recorded on sampled operating days with the latest versions the manufacturer had published by then.
Check that each update or repair in the period was followed by a recorded remote identification and geo-awareness check.

Output:
A list of aircraft with maintenance overdue or done outside the manufacturer's instructions.
A list of non-listed parts or non-allowed payloads fitted.
A list of operating days flown on outdated software or without a post-update check.

title.en: Collect each aircraft model's maintenance instructions, replaceable parts and allowed payloads

description.en: The guidance on class conformity makes the operator responsible for keeping each aircraft compliant throughout its life: replacing a part is not a modification if the part is original or matches the manufacturer's list of replaceable parts, a payload the manufacturer does not allow is forbidden, and maintenance outside the instructions invalidates class conformity. Gather the manufacturer's documents for every model in the fleet.

evidenceHint.en: Per-model file holding the manufacturer's maintenance instructions, replaceable parts list and allowed payload list, with document versions

text.en: List every aircraft model in the fleet register.
Obtain the current maintenance instructions for each model from the manufacturer.
Obtain the list of replaceable parts and the allowed payloads for each model.
Record each document's version and date and file it by model.

title.en: Schedule and record each aircraft's maintenance against the manufacturer's instructions

description.en: Carry out inspections, part replacements and battery care at the intervals the manufacturer sets, using only original or listed parts. Record each task against the aircraft's serial number, and track battery cycles so swollen or worn batteries are retired before they fail in flight.

evidenceHint.en: Maintenance records per aircraft showing tasks done, intervals, parts used with their part numbers and battery cycle counts

text.en: Schedule each aircraft's maintenance tasks at the manufacturer's intervals.
Fit only original parts or parts on the manufacturer's replaceable parts list.
Record each task, part number and the person who did it against the serial number.
Record battery cycles and retire any battery that is swollen or past the manufacturer's limit.

title.en: Update aircraft and remote-station software to the manufacturer's latest published version

description.en: Before each operating day, check for software the manufacturer has published for the aircraft and remote station, install it, and record the versions. After any update or repair, confirm the remote identification system still carries the operator string without error and that geo-awareness data is loaded, because updates and repairs can reset both.

evidenceHint.en: Software version record per aircraft and remote station, and the post-update remote ID and geo-awareness check record

text.en: Check the manufacturer's release channel for new aircraft and remote-station software.
Install published updates only from the manufacturer, never third-party firmware.
Record the installed versions for the aircraft and remote station.
Re-check remote ID shows the operator string without error after the update.
Re-load geo-awareness data if the update cleared it, and record the check.

title.en: Halt a payload or modification that the manufacturer does not allow before it flies

description.en: Before any payload is fitted or any change is made to an aircraft, check it against the manufacturer's allowed payloads and instructions and the MTOM. A change that is not foreseen by the manufacturer removes the aircraft's class conformity, so refuse it, or quarantine the aircraft in the fleet register and route it to the category its new state allows.

evidenceHint.en: Payload and change request record showing the check against allowed payloads and MTOM, and the decision taken

text.en: Compare the proposed payload or change with the manufacturer's allowed list.
Weigh the aircraft with the payload and compare it with the MTOM.
Approve only payloads and changes the manufacturer allows within the MTOM.
Quarantine the aircraft in the fleet register when a non-allowed change has been made.

title.en: Audit maintenance, parts and software records against the manufacturer's instructions each quarter

description.en: Each quarter sample aircraft and compare their maintenance records with the manufacturer's intervals, their parts with the replaceable parts list, their payloads with the allowed list, and their software versions on operating days with what the manufacturer had published. Raise a finding for each gap.

evidenceHint.en: Quarterly maintenance audit listing aircraft sampled, overdue tasks, non-listed parts, non-allowed payloads and outdated software found

text.en: Select at least three aircraft, including the most flown in the quarter.
Compare their maintenance records with the manufacturer's intervals.
Compare parts and payload records with the manufacturer's lists.
Compare software versions on sampled operating days with the manufacturer's releases.
Raise a finding for each gap with an owner and a due date.

templates.title: Open-category procedures, flight assignment and support personnel
templates.description: Open-category flights run on procedures fitted to the work and its risk, written down once the operator has more than one remote pilot, with one remote pilot named for every flight, trained support staff and radio use that causes no harmful interference.
templates.objective: To ensure every open-category flight runs on the operator's own procedures, with one named remote pilot, trained support staff and radio use that interferes with nothing.
templates.successCriteria:
Approved, dated procedures cover each type of open-category work the operator does, in writing once it employs more than one remote pilot.
A current list names every person in the operation and the duties assigned to each.
Every flight log names one designated remote pilot, and none records control handed to another command unit in flight.
Every observer and other support person holds a dated record of the operator's on-the-job training.
No aircraft or controller runs radio frequency or power settings other than those the manufacturer provides.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the operator's open-category procedures with their version history and approval dates.
Obtain the list of personnel and assigned duties, and the HR or contractor list for the same date.
Obtain flight logs for the period and the on-the-job training records for observers and other support staff.
Obtain the radio and link settings recorded for each aircraft and controller.

Analysis:
Compare the work types in the flight logs with the procedures and note work done without a procedure that covers it.
Reconcile the personnel list with the HR or contractor list and find people missing from either.
Sample flight logs for a single designated remote pilot and for any hand-over of control during flight.
Trace each observer or support person named in the sampled logs to a training record dated before the flight.
Compare recorded radio settings with the manufacturer's instructions for each model.

Output:
A list of work types flown without a procedure, and of procedures past their review date.
The personnel named in flight logs who are absent from the duties list or have no training record.
Any flight without a designated pilot, any in-flight hand-over and any non-standard radio setting found.

title.en: List each type of open-category work the operator flies and the risks its procedure must cover

description.en: Procedures have to fit the operation and its risk, so start from what the operator actually does: roof and mast inspections, filming, mapping, training flights. For each type, record the subcategory it is flown in, the usual environment, the aircraft used and the main hazards. This inventory is what the procedures are written against and what a later review compares the flight logs with.

evidenceHint.en: Inventory of open-category work types with subcategory, environment, aircraft and main hazards for each, dated

text.en: Pull the jobs flown in the last twelve months from the flight logs and booking records.
Group them into work types and note the subcategory each is flown in.
Record the usual environment, aircraft model and payload for each work type.
List the main hazards per type, such as people nearby, obstacles, wind or radio clutter.
Date the inventory and name the person who compiled it.

title.en: Write the open-category operations procedures and the list of personnel and duties

description.en: AMC1 UAS.OPEN.050(1) says written procedures are not needed when the operator is also the only remote pilot, but are expected once more than one pilot flies for it, together with a list of personnel and their assigned duties. Write procedures for each work type in the inventory, based on the manufacturer's instructions, and keep the duties list beside them so it is clear who plans, flies, observes and maintains.

evidenceHint.en: Approved open-category procedures with version and approval date, and the current personnel and duties list

text.en: Write a procedure for each work type covering planning, pre-flight, flight, post-flight and abnormal events.
Base each procedure on the manufacturer's instructions for the aircraft it uses.
List every person in the operation with the duties they are assigned.
Record how a pilot obtains the geographical zone information for the job.
Approve the procedures and the list, and record the version and date.

title.en: Restrict open-category aircraft and controllers to the manufacturer's radio settings

description.en: The operator must make sure every operation uses the radio spectrum efficiently and causes no harmful interference. In practice that means flying only with the command link, frequencies and transmit power the manufacturer provides for the market, with no third-party boosters, antennas or region hacks. Record the settings per aircraft and controller and forbid changes outside the manufacturer's options.

evidenceHint.en: Register of radio and link settings per aircraft and controller, and the procedure line forbidding non-standard changes

text.en: Record the link type, frequency band and region setting of every aircraft and controller.
Check each setting against the manufacturer's instructions for the country of use.
Remove any third-party amplifier, antenna or firmware patch that alters transmit power.
Add a procedure line forbidding radio changes outside the manufacturer's options.
Re-record the settings after any controller swap or firmware update.

title.en: Assign one designated remote pilot to every open-category flight before it starts

description.en: The operator designates a remote pilot for each flight, and GM1 UAS.OPEN.050(3) adds that control may not be handed to another command unit during an open-category flight. Make the designation part of planning: the flight is not released until one pilot is named, and the log records that the same person flew it from take-off to landing.

evidenceHint.en: Flight plans and logs naming one designated remote pilot per flight, with no in-flight hand-over recorded

text.en: Name the designated remote pilot in the flight plan before the flight is released.
Check the named pilot holds competency for the subcategory of the job.
Brief the crew that control stays with the designated pilot for the whole flight.
Record in the flight log that the designated pilot flew from take-off to landing.
Treat any change of pilot as a new flight with a new designation.

title.en: Train observers and other open-category support staff on the operator's procedures

description.en: People who support a flight without being its remote pilot, such as observers or ground crew, must complete an on-the-job training course developed by the operator and be fully familiar with its procedures and the manufacturer's instructions. Write the course, deliver it before anyone supports a flight, and keep a dated record per person.

evidenceHint.en: On-the-job training course outline and dated completion records for each observer and support person

text.en: Write an on-the-job training outline covering duties, procedures and the manufacturer's instructions.
Cover how an observer stays alongside the pilot and calls hazards clearly.
Deliver the training before the person supports their first flight.
Record the date, trainer and topics for each person trained.
Refresh the training when procedures or aircraft types change.

title.en: Review the open-category procedures against flight logs and incidents each year

description.en: Procedures drift from practice. Once a year, compare the procedures with what the logs show was actually flown and with the incidents and near misses recorded, and revise any procedure that no longer matches the work, the aircraft or the risk. Update the personnel list in the same pass.

evidenceHint.en: Annual review record listing procedures checked, gaps found and revisions approved, with the updated personnel list

text.en: Compare the year's work types in the flight logs with the procedure set.
Read the year's incidents and near misses for causes a procedure should address.
Revise each procedure that no longer fits the work, aircraft or risk.
Update the personnel and duties list to match current staff.
Record the review, the revisions made and the new approval date.

templates.title: Pre-flight checks and flight conduct in the open category
templates.description: Before every open-category flight the remote pilot checks their own competency, the zones, the site, the aircraft and its payload, and during it stays fit, in visual line of sight, below 120 m and clear of manned traffic and emergency response.
templates.objective: To ensure every open-category flight starts only after the checks UAS.OPEN.060 requires and is flown within its height, sight and fitness limits.
templates.successCriteria:
Every open-category flight log shows the pre-flight checklist completed before take-off, including payload mass within the manufacturer's and the class limit.
No track or log shows a flight above 120 m from the closest point of the surface, other than within 15 m above an obstacle at its owner's request.
Every flight was flown in visual line of sight by a pilot who declared themselves fit, with any observer standing alongside.
Every flight at night records the green flashing light switched on.
Every encounter with low-level manned traffic is logged with the action taken.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the open-category pre-flight checklist and the flight logs and track or telemetry exports for the period.
Obtain the permissions on file from entities responsible for obstacles taller than 105 m.
Obtain incident and near-miss reports for the period.

Analysis:
Sample flight logs and confirm each checklist item, including the payload mass and battery reserve, was completed before take-off.
Read the sampled tracks for maximum height above the surface and compare any height above 120 m with an obstacle permission.
Compare sampled flights with sunset times and check night flights record the green light on.
Check sampled logs for the pilot's fitness declaration and for observers positioned alongside the pilot.
Compare manned-traffic encounters in incident reports with the logs and the action recorded.

Output:
The proportion of sampled flights with a complete pre-flight checklist.
A list of height breaches without an obstacle permission and night flights without the light recorded.
Any flight without a fitness declaration, and any manned-traffic encounter missing from the log.

title.en: Define the open-category pre-flight checklist from UAS.OPEN.060 and the manufacturer's instructions

description.en: Turn the pilot's pre-flight duties into one checklist: competency held and proof carried, current zone information, a walk-round of the site for obstacles, people, roads and critical infrastructure (AMC1 UAS.OPEN.060(1)(c)), weather within the manufacturer's limits, aircraft fit to fly, payload secured and within both the manufacturer's MTOM and the class limit, battery enough for the job plus a reserve, and lost-link recovery set for the site (AMC1 UAS.OPEN.060(1)(d)).

evidenceHint.en: Approved open-category pre-flight checklist with each item traced to UAS.OPEN.060 or its AMC, with version and date

text.en: List the pre-flight duties of UAS.OPEN.060(1) as checklist items.
Add the site walk-round items from AMC1 UAS.OPEN.060(1)(c).
Add payload, battery reserve and lost-link recovery items from AMC1 UAS.OPEN.060(1)(d).
Add the weather limits from the manufacturer's instructions for each model.
Approve the checklist and record its version and approval date.

title.en: Set the 120 m height limit and the tall-obstacle rule in each open-category flight plan

description.en: An open-category aircraft stays within 120 m of the closest point of the earth's surface, measured with the terrain. Within 50 m of an artificial obstacle taller than 105 m it may climb to 15 m above the obstacle, but only at the request of the entity responsible for it, and GM1 UAS.OPEN.010 asks for that permission to be explicit. A geographical zone with a lower limit wins. Put the applicable ceiling in each flight plan and set it in the aircraft's height limiter where it has one.

evidenceHint.en: Flight plans stating the height ceiling, height-limiter settings, and any obstacle owner's written request on file

text.en: Work out the ceiling for the site from the terrain, the 120 m rule and any lower zone limit.
Write the ceiling into the flight plan before the flight is released.
Set the aircraft's height limiter to the ceiling where the model has one.
File the written request of the obstacle's owner before using the 15 m allowance.
Record the maximum height reached in the flight log after landing.

title.en: Brief remote pilots on fitness, visual line of sight and manned traffic before each open-category day

description.en: During flight the pilot must not be under the influence of psychoactive substances or alcohol or unfit through injury, fatigue, medication or sickness, must keep the aircraft in sight with a thorough scan of the airspace and stop if the flight poses a risk. GM1 UAS.OPEN.060(2)(b) tells a pilot who sees low-level manned traffic to descend, for example below 10 m, keep at least 500 m away or land. Brief this at the start of each flying day, with the one-aircraft-at-a-time rule of AMC1 UAS.OPEN.060(2)(d).

evidenceHint.en: Daily briefing record with the pilot's fitness declaration and acknowledgement of the sight, traffic and emergency-area rules

text.en: Ask each pilot to declare they are fit and free of alcohol, drugs, fatigue and medication effects.
Remind pilots to keep the aircraft in sight and scan the airspace throughout.
Brief the response to low-level manned traffic: descend, keep at least 500 m away or land.
Confirm pilots fly one aircraft at a time and never from a vehicle they are driving.
Remind pilots to keep clear of emergency response unless the responders allow it.
Record the briefing and each pilot's declaration with the date.

title.en: Log each open-category flight with its completed checks, maximum height and any deviation

description.en: The flight log is the evidence that the duties were met. After each flight record the designated pilot, aircraft, site, times, maximum height, completed checklist, whether it was flown at night with the green flashing light on, any observer used and anything abnormal such as manned traffic, a lost link or a person entering the area. Attach the track or telemetry export where the aircraft produces one.

evidenceHint.en: Open-category flight log entries with checklist, maximum height, night light status, observer and deviations, plus track export

text.en: Record the pilot, aircraft, site and take-off and landing times.
Tick the pre-flight checklist in the log before take-off.
Record the maximum height reached and whether the flight was at night with the light on.
Note any observer used and confirm they stood alongside the pilot.
Describe any manned traffic, lost link or other deviation and the action taken.

title.en: Sample open-category flight logs each month for skipped checks and height or sight breaches

description.en: Pick a sample of the month's open-category flights and check each log against its track: was the checklist completed before take-off, did the aircraft stay within the planned ceiling, was it flown in sight and, at night, with the green light on, and were deviations recorded and handled. Raise a finding for each gap and follow it to closure.

evidenceHint.en: Monthly sample worksheet listing flights reviewed, checks found missing, height or sight breaches and findings raised

text.en: Select at least five flights from the month across different pilots and sites.
Confirm each checklist was completed before the recorded take-off time.
Compare the maximum height in each track with the planned ceiling.
Check night flights record the green flashing light switched on.
Raise a finding for each gap with an owner and due date, and file the worksheet.

templates.title: Remote identification and geo-awareness active and updated
templates.description: Every class aircraft that must fly with active and updated direct remote identification and geo-awareness does so: the operator provides current zone data for each location, and the pilot loads it and checks remote ID carries the right operator string before each flight.
templates.objective: To ensure no C1, C2 or C3 aircraft flies in the open category without remote identification active and current and geo-awareness loaded with the latest zone data.
templates.successCriteria:
For every operating location the operator has downloaded the latest zone data from the State's official source and recorded its version and date.
Every flight log of a C1, C2 or C3 aircraft records geo-awareness updated and remote ID checked active with no error shown before take-off.
Every remote ID broadcast checked carries the operator's current registration number.
After every firmware update, repair or aircraft swap, remote ID and geo-awareness were re-verified before the next flight.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the record of zone data downloads per State and location, with versions and dates.
Obtain flight logs for C1, C2 and C3 aircraft for the period.
Obtain the firmware update and repair records and the remote ID verification records that follow them.
Obtain a remote ID receiver capture or app screenshot for a sample of aircraft.

Analysis:
Compare the zone data date used for each sampled flight with the latest data the State published before that flight.
Check each sampled log records geo-awareness updated and remote ID active before take-off.
Read the remote ID capture for the operator number and compare it with the current registration.
Trace each firmware update or repair to a remote ID and geo-awareness re-verification before the next flight.

Output:
A list of flights made with outdated zone data or with remote ID or geo-awareness checks missing.
Any aircraft broadcasting a wrong or outdated operator number.
Any update or repair followed by a flight without re-verification.

title.en: Identify which open-category aircraft must fly with remote ID and geo-awareness active

description.en: UAS.OPEN.020(5)(d), UAS.OPEN.030(3) and UAS.OPEN.040(4)(c) and (d) require a C1, C2 or C3 aircraft to fly with active and updated direct remote identification and geo-awareness. Mark each aircraft in the fleet register with whether the rule applies, which remote ID and geo-awareness functions it has, and how its manufacturer says data is loaded, so the checks below are applied to the right aircraft.

evidenceHint.en: Fleet register extract marking each aircraft's class, whether the remote ID and geo-awareness rule applies, and its loading method

text.en: List every aircraft flown in the open category with its class label.
Mark each C1, C2 and C3 aircraft as needing active remote ID and geo-awareness.
Record how the manufacturer says the operator number is loaded into remote ID.
Record how the manufacturer says zone data is loaded into geo-awareness.
Note aircraft that have the functions without the rule applying, and use them anyway.

title.en: Obtain the latest geographical zone data for each open-category operating location

description.en: AMC1 UAS.OPEN.050(4)(c) expects the operator to download the latest version of the geographical data and make it available to the pilot for loading. Before each operation, take the data from the State's official source for that location, record which version and date was taken, and hand it to the pilot with the job pack.

evidenceHint.en: Zone data download log per location with source, version and date, attached to each job pack

text.en: Identify the official zone data source for the State of operation.
Download the latest data covering the job's location before the operation.
Record the source, version and download date in the job pack.
Send the data or the instruction to load it to the designated pilot.
Re-download when the State publishes an update before the job is flown.

title.en: Load zone data and verify remote ID before each flight of a C1, C2 or C3 aircraft

description.en: Before take-off the pilot updates geo-awareness with the data for the location (AMC1 UAS.OPEN.060(1)(d)) and checks direct remote ID is active and up to date. The remote ID system checks the operator number for integrity and shows an error if it is inconsistent, so an error on start-up means the aircraft does not fly. Record both checks in the flight log.

evidenceHint.en: Flight log entries recording geo-awareness data loaded and remote ID checked active with no error, per flight

text.en: Load the zone data supplied for the location into the aircraft or its app.
Confirm the geo-awareness function shows the data loaded and no positioning warning.
Check remote ID is switched on and carries the operator's current registration number.
Ground the aircraft if remote ID shows an error message on start-up.
Record both checks in the flight log before take-off.

title.en: Re-verify remote ID and geo-awareness after every firmware update, repair or aircraft swap

description.en: An update, a repair or swapping a flight controller can clear or change the operator string or the zone data. Make re-verification part of returning an aircraft to service: reload the operator number if needed, confirm with a remote ID receiver that the broadcast carries it, reload zone data, and record the check before the aircraft flies again.

evidenceHint.en: Return-to-service record showing remote ID broadcast checked with a receiver and zone data reloaded after each update or repair

text.en: Flag the aircraft for re-verification whenever firmware is updated or it is repaired.
Reload the operator number and secret digits if the update cleared them.
Check with a remote ID receiver app that the broadcast shows the operator number.
Reload the current zone data and confirm geo-awareness accepts it.
Record the re-verification before releasing the aircraft to flight.

title.en: Spot-check remote ID broadcasts and zone data currency across the open-category fleet quarterly

description.en: Logs say what pilots ticked; a spot-check shows what the aircraft actually broadcast. Each quarter, power up a sample of C1, C2 and C3 aircraft, capture their remote ID with a receiver app and check the zone data version loaded against the latest the State has published. Raise findings for any mismatch.

evidenceHint.en: Quarterly spot-check sheet with receiver captures, loaded zone data versions and findings per aircraft

text.en: Select a sample of C1, C2 and C3 aircraft covering each model in the fleet.
Capture each aircraft's remote ID broadcast with a receiver app.
Compare the broadcast operator number with the current registration.
Compare the loaded zone data version with the latest the State published.
Raise a finding for each mismatch and record the sheet with its date.

templates.title: Class label, declaration of conformity and modification control
templates.description: Each class aircraft flown in the open category travels with its EU declaration of conformity naming the class and carries its class label, and any modification, payload or repair outside the manufacturer's allowance takes it out of the open category.
templates.objective: To ensure every class aircraft flown in the open category is conformant on paper and in fact, and that a change voiding its class leaves it flying only in the specific category.
templates.successCriteria:
Every C0 to C4 aircraft flown in the open category has its EU declaration of conformity on file, naming its class.
Every such aircraft carries its class identification label, photographed and checked at receipt and after repair.
Every modification, non-standard payload or repair is assessed before the aircraft flies again, and the assessment is recorded.
No aircraft whose class conformity was lost has flown in the open category since; its label is removed and it is restricted to specific-category use.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the declaration of conformity file and label photographs for every class aircraft in the open-category fleet.
Obtain the modification and payload change records and repair records for the period.
Obtain the flight logs for any aircraft whose conformity was assessed as lost.

Analysis:
Reconcile the fleet register with the declarations on file and note any class aircraft without one or with a class that does not match its label.
Inspect a sample of aircraft and compare the label in place with the photograph on file.
Read each modification, payload and repair record for an assessment made before the next flight, against the manufacturer's allowed parts and payloads.
Check the flight logs of aircraft assessed as no longer conformant for any open-category flight after the assessment date.

Output:
A list of class aircraft missing a declaration or a label.
A list of changes made without a prior assessment.
Any open-category flight by an aircraft whose class conformity had been lost.

title.en: Collect the EU declaration of conformity and class label evidence for each open-category aircraft

description.en: UAS.OPEN.050(6) requires a C0 to C4 aircraft flown in the open category to be accompanied by its EU declaration of conformity referencing the class, with the class identification label affixed. At receipt, file the declaration against the serial number, photograph the label in place and check the two agree before the aircraft is released for open-category work.

evidenceHint.en: Declaration of conformity per serial number, label photograph and receipt check record for each class aircraft

text.en: Obtain the EU declaration of conformity from the manufacturer or importer for each aircraft.
Check the declaration names the aircraft's class and model.
Photograph the class identification label in place on the aircraft.
File the declaration and photograph against the serial number in the fleet register.
Release the aircraft for open-category work only when both are on file and agree.

title.en: Define the change gate for modifications, payloads and repairs on open-category aircraft

description.en: The AMC to UAS.OPEN.020(5), UAS.OPEN.030(3) and UAS.OPEN.040(4) make the operator responsible for keeping a class aircraft compliant for its life: a replacement part is not a modification when it is original or on the manufacturer's replaceable-parts list, but a payload the manufacturer does not allow, a change it did not foresee or maintenance outside its instructions invalidates the class. Write the gate every change must pass before the aircraft flies again.

evidenceHint.en: Approved change-gate procedure listing allowed parts and payloads per model and the assessment step before release

text.en: List the manufacturer's replaceable parts and allowed payloads for each model in the fleet.
State that any part, payload or change outside those lists is a modification.
Require an assessment and sign-off before a changed aircraft flies again.
State that an aircraft whose class is invalidated leaves the open category.
Approve the procedure and record its version and date.

title.en: Assess each open-category aircraft change before release and record the outcome

description.en: Apply the change gate whenever a part is replaced, a payload is fitted, firmware from outside the manufacturer is considered or a repair is made. The assessment records what changed, whether it is within the manufacturer's allowance, and either releases the aircraft for the open category or moves it to the conformity-lost route.

evidenceHint.en: Change assessment records per aircraft naming the change, the allowance checked and the release or conformity-lost decision

text.en: Record the change, the part or payload used and who made it.
Compare it with the manufacturer's replaceable-parts and allowed-payload lists.
Release the aircraft for open-category work if the change is within the allowance.
Send the aircraft to the conformity-lost route if it is not.
Sign and date the assessment before the aircraft flies again.

title.en: Remove the class label and restrict an open-category aircraft whose conformity is lost

description.en: When a change invalidates class conformity, the AMC says the class identification label must be removed and the aircraft may then be operated only in the specific category. Remove the label, change the aircraft's status in the fleet register so it cannot be assigned to an open-category job, and record what specific-category basis, if any, it will fly under.

evidenceHint.en: Fleet register status change, label removal photograph and record of the specific-category basis or retirement

text.en: Remove the class identification label from the aircraft and photograph the result.
Change the aircraft's register status so open-category jobs cannot select it.
Record whether it will fly under a specific-category authorisation or be retired.
Tell the flight planners that the aircraft has left the open category.
Keep the change assessment that triggered the restriction on its record.

title.en: Inspect a sample of open-category aircraft each quarter for labels, papers and unrecorded changes

description.en: Walk the hangar or kit store each quarter and check a sample of open-category aircraft against their records: label in place and matching the photograph, declaration on file, and no part, payload or modification fitted that has no change assessment. Raise findings and ground any aircraft with an unrecorded change until it is assessed.

evidenceHint.en: Quarterly inspection sheet per aircraft sampled, with label check, declaration check, unrecorded changes and findings

text.en: Select a sample of open-category aircraft covering each model and class.
Compare the label on each aircraft with the photograph on file.
Confirm a declaration of conformity naming the class is on file for each.
Look for parts or payloads fitted with no change assessment recorded.
Ground any aircraft with an unrecorded change and raise a finding.

templates.title: Open-category competency validity and revalidation
templates.description: The A1/A3 online competency and the A2 certificate each last five years, and are revalidated before they expire through a fresh exam or a refresher training from the competent authority or its designated entity; a lapsed credential takes the pilot off that subcategory.
templates.objective: To ensure no pilot flies an open-category subcategory on an expired credential and each revalidation takes the route UAS.OPEN.070 allows at that point in the credential's life.
templates.successCriteria:
Every A1/A3 proof and A2 certificate on the roster has an issue date and an expiry five years later.
Alerts went out at six and at three months before each expiry in the period.
Every credential that expired in the period was revalidated before expiry, or its holder was withdrawn from that subcategory on the expiry date.
Every revalidation after expiry was by examination, and every revalidation inside validity was by examination or by a refresher from the competent authority or its designated entity.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the pilot roster with each open-category credential's issue and expiry dates.
Obtain the alert log and the revalidation records, including the issuer and route of each.
Obtain rostering records and flight logs for pilots whose credentials expired in the period.
Obtain the list of revalidation routes each issuing State's competent authority or designated entity offers.

Analysis:
Recompute each expiry from the issue date and compare it with the roster.
Check alerts were sent at the six- and three-month points for every credential expiring in the period.
For each revalidation, compare its date with the expiry and confirm the route taken was allowed at that date.
Check rostering and flight logs for any open-category flight by a pilot after their credential expired and before it was revalidated.
Compare the new proof on file for each revalidation with the issuer and identification number of the old one.

Output:
A list of credentials with a wrong expiry date or no alert sent.
Any revalidation made by a route not allowed at that point.
Any flight made on an expired credential.

title.en: Record the issue and expiry date of every A1/A3 proof and A2 certificate on the roster

description.en: UAS.OPEN.070(1) makes both the A1/A3 online theoretical competency and the A2 certificate valid for five years. Record the issue date and the issuing authority for every credential held, compute the expiry from the issue date rather than copying it from the pilot, and keep a copy of the proof itself.

evidenceHint.en: Roster extract with issue date, expiry date and issuing authority for every open-category credential, with copies of the proofs

text.en: Collect a copy of each pilot's A1/A3 proof and A2 certificate.
Record the issuing authority and the issue date shown on each.
Compute the expiry date as five years after the issue date.
Flag any credential whose shown expiry differs from the computed one.
Store the copies against the pilot's roster entry.

title.en: Schedule open-category credential expiry alerts at six and three months

description.en: Inside its validity a credential can be revalidated by demonstrating competency again or by a refresher training provided by the competent authority or its designated entity; after expiry only the examination route remains (UAS.OPEN.070(2) and (3)). Alerts early enough keep the cheaper route open. Set alerts at six and three months and tell the pilot which routes their issuing State offers.

evidenceHint.en: Alert schedule configuration and alert log showing six- and three-month notices sent for each expiring credential

text.en: Set an alert six months before each open-category credential expires.
Set a second alert three months before expiry.
Include in the alert the revalidation routes the issuing State offers.
Copy the pilot's manager so rostering can plan around the revalidation.
Log each alert sent with its date.

title.en: Complete each open-category credential revalidation by an allowed route and file the new proof

description.en: Help the pilot book the revalidation before expiry: an exam, or a refresher where the competent authority or its designated entity provides one. Once done, file the new proof, update the issue and expiry dates on the roster, and record the route used so a reviewer can see it was allowed at that date.

evidenceHint.en: Revalidation record naming the route, provider and date, with the new proof and updated roster dates

text.en: Book the exam or refresher with the competent authority or its designated entity.
Confirm the route chosen is allowed for the credential's current status.
File the new proof once the revalidation is complete.
Update the roster with the new issue and expiry dates.
Record the route, provider and completion date.

title.en: Withdraw a pilot from a subcategory on the day their open-category credential expires

description.en: A pilot whose A1/A3 proof or A2 certificate has expired no longer holds the competency the subcategory requires. On the expiry date, remove the pilot from rostering for that subcategory, cancel any job they are booked to fly in it, and restore them only when a new proof is filed.

evidenceHint.en: Roster change log showing the withdrawal on the expiry date and reinstatement after revalidation

text.en: Check daily for open-category credentials expiring that day.
Remove each affected pilot from rostering for that subcategory.
Reassign any job they were booked to fly in it.
Tell the pilot that they are withdrawn and what is needed to return.
Reinstate the pilot only after the new proof is filed.

title.en: Review open-category credential lapses and revalidation routes each quarter

description.en: Each quarter, look back at the credentials that fell due: were alerts sent, was every one revalidated in time or the pilot withdrawn, and did any pilot fly after expiry. Record the findings and fix the alerting or rostering where it failed.

evidenceHint.en: Quarterly review record of credentials due, alerts sent, revalidations made, withdrawals and any flight on an expired credential

text.en: List the open-category credentials that expired or fell due in the quarter.
Confirm each received its six- and three-month alerts.
Confirm each was revalidated in time or its holder withdrawn on the expiry date.
Search flight logs for any flight by a pilot after their credential expired.
Record the findings and the fixes made to alerting or rostering.

templates.title: Involved persons informed of the risks and consenting (A2 and A3)
templates.description: In subcategories A2 and A3 every person present in the area of the operation as an involved person has been told the risks and has explicitly agreed to take part; anybody else is uninvolved and the distances apply to them.
templates.objective: To ensure everyone treated as involved in an A2 or A3 operation was briefed on its risks and explicitly agreed to take part, and that nobody else is counted as involved.
templates.successCriteria:
Every A2 and A3 operation with involved persons has a briefing and consent record naming each person, made before the flight.
Every briefing covered the risks, where to stand and what to do if the aircraft behaves unexpectedly.
No consent relies on a public address announcement, a ticket statement or an e-mail alone.
People who declined or arrived after the briefing were treated as uninvolved until briefed, and the logs show the distances kept from them.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the operator's involved-persons procedure and briefing script.
Obtain the consent records and the flight logs for A2 and A3 operations in the period.
Obtain incident reports involving people at A2 or A3 sites.

Analysis:
Compare the briefing script with the elements GM1 Article 2(18) describes: explicit consent, clear instructions and safety precautions, and a check that they were understood.
Sample A2 and A3 operations and match each person named as involved in the log to a consent record timed before the flight.
Read the consent records for any reliance on announcements, tickets or messages instead of a direct briefing.
Compare incident reports with the consent records for people who were close to the aircraft without having consented.

Output:
A list of operations where people were treated as involved without a consent record.
Any consent obtained by a channel the guidance says does not suffice.
Any incident involving a person who was close to the aircraft but not briefed.

title.en: Define who counts as an involved person in A2 and A3 operations

description.en: GM1 Article 2(18) treats a person as involved only when, before the flight, they have explicitly agreed to take part (verbal agreement is enough) and have received clear instructions and safety precautions. They must be free to decide, broadly understand the risks and not be excluded from the activity if they decline. Spectators at events are uninvolved. Write this into the procedure so crews apply one test.

evidenceHint.en: Procedure section defining involved and uninvolved persons for A2 and A3, with its approval date

text.en: State that a person is involved only after a briefing and their explicit agreement.
State that agreement may be verbal but must be given to the operator or pilot directly.
State that anyone who declines must be able to stay in the activity as uninvolved.
State that event spectators and passers-by are uninvolved persons.
Approve the definition and record the version and date.

title.en: Write the A2 and A3 involved-persons briefing and consent record

description.en: Prepare a short briefing that covers the operation's risks, where involved people must stand, how the aircraft may behave if something goes wrong and what each person should do. Pair it with a consent record that names each person, the time and how they agreed. The guidance warns that announcements, ticket statements, e-mails or messages are not enough, so the record captures a direct briefing.

evidenceHint.en: Approved briefing script and blank consent record naming person, time, briefer and form of agreement

text.en: Write the risks of the operation in plain words a non-pilot will understand.
Describe safe positions and what to do on a fly-away or forced landing.
Add two or three simple questions to check the briefing was understood.
Design a consent record capturing name, time, briefer and how consent was given.
Approve the script and record and issue them with the A2 and A3 job packs.

title.en: Brief each involved person and record their consent before an A2 or A3 flight

description.en: On site, before the first flight, the pilot or crew briefs each person who will be treated as involved, asks the check questions and records their explicit agreement. Anyone who declines, or does not understand, is treated as uninvolved and the distance rules of the subcategory apply to them.

evidenceHint.en: Completed consent records for each A2 and A3 operation, timed before the first flight, with decliners noted

text.en: Deliver the briefing to each person before the first flight.
Ask the check questions and correct any misunderstanding.
Record each person's explicit agreement with the time.
Note anyone who declines and treat them as uninvolved.
Attach the consent record to the flight log for the operation.

title.en: Brief people who arrive during an A2 or A3 operation before treating them as involved

description.en: Sites change: a new contractor arrives, a client walks out to watch. Until a newcomer has been briefed and has agreed, they are an uninvolved person and the subcategory's distances apply. Pause or move the aircraft as needed, brief the person, record their consent and only then treat them as involved.

evidenceHint.en: Consent records for late arrivals with times, and flight log notes of any pause or repositioning

text.en: Ask the observer to watch for people arriving at the site.
Keep the subcategory's distances from any newcomer who has not been briefed.
Pause or reposition the aircraft if a newcomer comes too close.
Brief the newcomer and record their consent with the time.
Note the pause or repositioning in the flight log.

title.en: Review A2 and A3 consent records against flight logs and incidents each month

description.en: Each month, sample A2 and A3 operations and check that everyone the log treats as involved has a consent record made before the flight, that no consent relied on an announcement or message, and that incidents involving people show the person had been briefed. Raise findings and refresh crew training where the records fall short.

evidenceHint.en: Monthly review sheet of operations sampled, consent gaps, channels used and findings raised

text.en: Select A2 and A3 operations from the month across different crews.
Match each person treated as involved to a consent record timed before the flight.
Flag any consent given by announcement, ticket statement or message.
Compare incidents involving people with the consent records.
Raise findings and arrange refresher briefings for crews with gaps.

templates.title: Overflight limits in subcategory A1
templates.description: In subcategory A1 assemblies of people are never overflown; with a C1 the pilot plans so no uninvolved person is expected to be overflown and cuts short any unexpected overflight, and follow-me mode is used only up to 50 m from the pilot.
templates.objective: To ensure every A1 flight keeps off assemblies of people and applies the overflight rule of its aircraft class, with follow-me use within 50 m of the pilot.
templates.successCriteria:
No A1 flight log, track or incident record shows an assembly of people overflown.
Every A1 flight with a C1 aircraft has a recorded site assessment showing the pilot reasonably expected no uninvolved person to be overflown.
Every unexpected overflight with a C1 is logged with the action taken to shorten it.
No A1 flight in follow-me mode went further than 50 m from the remote pilot.
Every A1 site used repeatedly has its assessment revised after any recorded unexpected overflight.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the A1 procedure, the flight plans with site assessments and the flight logs and tracks for the period.
Obtain incident reports for A1 operations.
Obtain the follow-me settings recorded for each aircraft used in follow-me mode.

Analysis:
Sample A1 flights and read the track against the site plan for passes over assemblies of people, such as events, markets or crowds.
For each sampled C1 flight, confirm a site assessment was made before take-off considering roads, paths, time of day and the ability to secure the site, as AMC1 UAS.OPEN.020(1) describes.
Read logs for unexpected overflights and the action taken to end them.
For sampled follow-me flights, compute the maximum distance from the pilot from the track and compare it with the recorded follow distance.
Compare incident reports with the logs for overflights the logs do not mention.

Output:
Any overflight of an assembly of people in the sample.
A list of C1 flights without a prior site assessment, and of unexpected overflights with no recorded response.
Any follow-me flight that exceeded 50 m from the pilot.

title.en: Write the A1 overflight rules for each aircraft class the operator flies in A1

description.en: UAS.OPEN.020(1) and (2) set different overflight rules by aircraft: with a C1 the pilot must reasonably expect that no uninvolved person will be overflown and must keep any unexpected overflight as short as possible; with a C0, a privately built aircraft under 250 g or an Article 20(a) legacy aircraft uninvolved people may be overflown. Assemblies of people are never overflown by any of them. Write the rule per class into the A1 procedure.

evidenceHint.en: A1 procedure section stating the overflight rule per aircraft class and the ban on overflying assemblies, with approval date

text.en: List the aircraft classes the operator flies in A1.
State for C1 aircraft that no uninvolved person may be expected to be overflown.
State for C0 and sub-250 g aircraft that uninvolved people may be overflown.
State for every class that assemblies of people are never overflown.
Approve the procedure section and record its version and date.

title.en: Assess each A1 site for uninvolved people before flying a C1 aircraft

description.en: AMC1 UAS.OPEN.020(1) asks the pilot of a C1 to assess the area before starting, taking into account the configuration of the site, such as roads, streets and pedestrian or cycle paths, the possibility of securing it and the time of day. Record the assessment so it is clear why the pilot expected no uninvolved person to be overflown.

evidenceHint.en: A1 site assessment record per C1 flight noting roads, paths, time of day, securing measures and the conclusion

text.en: Walk or view the site and note roads, streets and pedestrian or cycle paths.
Consider the time of day and how busy the area will be during the flight.
Decide what can be done to secure the area, such as cones or a helper.
Plan the flight path so it avoids places where people are likely to be.
Record the assessment and its conclusion before take-off.

title.en: Reduce and log any unexpected A1 overflight of an uninvolved person

description.en: If a person walks under a C1 aircraft unexpectedly, UAS.OPEN.020(1) requires the pilot to reduce the time of the overflight as much as possible, for example by moving the aircraft so the distance from the person grows or holding it over a place where nobody is. Make this the trained response and record every occurrence.

evidenceHint.en: A1 flight log entries for each unexpected overflight with time, action taken and duration

text.en: Move the aircraft away from the person as soon as they are below it.
Hold the aircraft over a clear area until the person has passed.
Do not resume the planned path over people until the area is clear again.
Record the time, action taken and how long the overflight lasted.
Report repeated overflights at one site so the site assessment is revised.

title.en: Limit A1 follow-me flights to 50 m from the remote pilot

description.en: UAS.OPEN.020(3) allows an A1 flight in follow-me mode, as an exception to keeping the aircraft in visual line of sight, only up to 50 m from the remote pilot. Set the follow distance and any range limit the aircraft offers before using follow-me, and confirm the flight stayed within 50 m.

evidenceHint.en: Follow-me configuration record per A1 aircraft and track checks showing the maximum distance from the pilot

text.en: Set the follow-me distance on the aircraft to 50 m or less.
Set any distance or range limit the aircraft offers to the same value.
Brief the pilot that follow-me must stop if the aircraft passes 50 m away.
Check the track after the flight for the maximum distance from the pilot.
Record the setting and the maximum distance in the flight log.

title.en: Sample A1 tracks each month for assemblies overflown and follow-me range

description.en: Each month, sample A1 flights and compare the tracks with the site plans and assessments: was any assembly of people overflown, did C1 flights stay off places people were expected, were unexpected overflights handled and logged, and did follow-me flights stay within 50 m. Raise findings for each breach.

evidenceHint.en: Monthly A1 sample worksheet with flights reviewed, overflight findings and follow-me range checks

text.en: Select a sample of the month's A1 flights across pilots and sites.
Overlay each track on the site plan and look for passes over assemblies.
Check each C1 flight has a site assessment made before take-off.
Check follow-me flights for a maximum distance above 50 m.
Raise a finding for each breach and file the worksheet.

templates.title: Aircraft eligible for subcategory A1
templates.description: Only aircraft that UAS.OPEN.020(5) or Article 20(a) admit fly in subcategory A1: privately built under 250 g, class C0, class C1 with remote ID and geo-awareness active, or a legacy aircraft under 250 g placed on the market before 1 January 2024.
templates.objective: To ensure every aircraft assigned to A1 work holds one of the bases A1 admits, and that payload never takes a sub-250 g aircraft over its limit.
templates.successCriteria:
Every aircraft assigned to A1 work in the period has an A1 eligibility basis recorded in the fleet register.
Every privately built A1 aircraft has a recorded MTOM under 250 g and a maximum speed under 19 m/s.
Every Article 20(a) aircraft has evidence it was placed on the market before 1 January 2024 and weighs under 250 g.
No sub-250 g aircraft flew A1 with a payload that took it to 250 g or more.
Every C1 assigned to A1 work had remote ID and geo-awareness reported working on the date it flew.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the fleet register with each aircraft's A1 eligibility basis, mass and speed figures.
Obtain purchase or market-date evidence for any Article 20(a) aircraft.
Obtain A1 job assignments and flight logs for the period, with payload records.
Obtain the weighing records and the declarations of conformity for C0 and C1 aircraft.

Analysis:
Trace each aircraft assigned to A1 work to an eligibility basis recorded before the assignment.
For privately built aircraft, compare the weighed MTOM with 250 g and the maximum speed with 19 m/s.
For Article 20(a) aircraft, check the date evidence and the mass.
For sub-250 g aircraft, compare the recorded payload mass with the margin below 250 g.
For C1 aircraft, check the flight logs record remote ID and geo-awareness working.

Output:
A list of aircraft that flew A1 without an eligibility basis.
Any privately built or legacy aircraft whose figures do not meet the A1 limits.
Any A1 flight where payload took a sub-250 g aircraft to 250 g or more.

title.en: Map each fleet aircraft to an A1 eligibility basis or mark it not eligible for A1

description.en: UAS.OPEN.020(5) admits four kinds of aircraft to A1: privately built with an MTOM under 250 g and a maximum operating speed under 19 m/s, class C0, class C1 flown with active and updated remote ID and geo-awareness, and, through Article 20(a), a non-class aircraft under 250 g placed on the market before 1 January 2024. Record which basis each aircraft holds, or that it holds none.

evidenceHint.en: Fleet register column showing the A1 basis per aircraft, or not eligible, with the date it was set

text.en: List every aircraft the operator might use for A1 work.
Record class C0 or C1 from the class label and declaration of conformity.
Record privately built aircraft under 250 g and 19 m/s as their own basis.
Record legacy aircraft under 250 g placed on the market before 1 January 2024 under Article 20(a).
Mark every other aircraft as not eligible for A1.

title.en: Weigh privately built and legacy A1 aircraft and record their mass and speed

description.en: The privately built and Article 20(a) bases depend on figures the operator must be able to show: an MTOM under 250 g, and for privately built aircraft a maximum operating speed under 19 m/s. Weigh each aircraft in its flying configuration, record its maximum speed from its build or test, and keep the purchase or market-date evidence for legacy aircraft.

evidenceHint.en: Weighing record, speed figure and market-date evidence per privately built or legacy A1 aircraft

text.en: Weigh each aircraft with battery and propellers fitted on calibrated scales.
Record the maximum operating speed from the build specification or a test flight.
Keep the purchase or market-date evidence for each legacy aircraft.
Mark the aircraft not eligible for A1 if any figure misses the limit.
Re-weigh after any change to the airframe or battery.

title.en: Check payload keeps each sub-250 g A1 aircraft under 250 g before flight

description.en: A camera, light or guard fitted to a sub-250 g aircraft can push it over the limit and out of the basis it flies under. Record the margin each sub-250 g aircraft has below 250 g, and check before every flight with an added payload that the total stays under the limit.

evidenceHint.en: Pre-flight payload mass checks for sub-250 g A1 aircraft, recorded in the flight log

text.en: Look up the aircraft's recorded mass and its margin below 250 g.
Weigh or look up the mass of any payload or accessory fitted.
Confirm the total stays below 250 g before take-off.
Remove the payload or change aircraft if the total reaches 250 g.
Record the check in the flight log.

title.en: Restrict A1 job assignment to aircraft with an A1 eligibility basis

description.en: Make the register drive planning: when a job is planned in A1, only aircraft whose A1 basis is recorded can be assigned, and a C1 can be assigned only while its remote ID and geo-awareness are working. Record the aircraft and basis in the flight plan.

evidenceHint.en: A1 flight plans naming the aircraft and its eligibility basis, and the planning rule that enforces it

text.en: Filter the aircraft offered for A1 jobs to those with an A1 basis recorded.
Exclude any C1 whose remote ID or geo-awareness is reported faulty.
Record the aircraft and its basis in each A1 flight plan.
Refuse a planned A1 job if no eligible aircraft is available.
Review the filter whenever the fleet register changes.

title.en: Reconcile A1 flights with the fleet register's eligibility bases each quarter

description.en: Each quarter, take the A1 flights flown and check every aircraft used held an A1 basis at the time, that privately built and legacy aircraft still meet their mass and speed figures, and that no payload took a sub-250 g aircraft over the limit. Raise findings and correct the register.

evidenceHint.en: Quarterly A1 reconciliation listing aircraft used, bases held, figures re-checked and findings

text.en: List every aircraft used for A1 flights in the quarter.
Confirm each held an A1 basis on the dates it flew.
Spot-check the mass of a sample of privately built and legacy aircraft.
Check payload records for flights by sub-250 g aircraft.
Raise findings and correct the register where it is wrong.

templates.title: Remote pilot competency for subcategory A1
templates.description: Every A1 pilot knows the manufacturer's instructions for the aircraft they fly, and a pilot flying a C1 has also completed the online training and passed the online theoretical examination and carries the proof.
templates.objective: To ensure every A1 pilot meets the competency their aircraft calls for: the manufacturer's instructions for all, and the online training and exam with proof carried for C1 pilots.
templates.successCriteria:
Every A1 pilot has a record of familiarisation with the manufacturer's instructions for each model they fly.
Every pilot who flew a C1 in A1 holds a valid A1/A3 proof of completion from the competent authority or its designated entity.
Every C1 flight log confirms the proof was carried.
No pilot without the proof was assigned to a C1 flight in A1.
Every A1/A3 proof on file shows its identification number, issuer and issue date, and was inside its five-year validity on each C1 flight.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the A1 pilot roster with familiarisation records per model and A1/A3 proofs.
Obtain A1 flight logs for the period showing pilot, aircraft class and proof carried.
Obtain the copies of the manufacturer's instructions used for familiarisation, with their revision dates.

Analysis:
For each sampled A1 flight, check the pilot has a familiarisation record for the model flown, dated before the flight.
For each sampled C1 flight, check the pilot held a valid A1/A3 proof on the flight date and the log confirms it was carried.
Compare the issuer of each proof with the competent authorities and designated entities of the Member States.
Search rostering for C1 assignments to pilots without a proof.
Compare each familiarisation date with the revision date of the instructions it used.

Output:
A list of A1 flights by pilots without a familiarisation record for the model.
Any C1 flight by a pilot without a valid A1/A3 proof, or with the proof not carried.
Any proof from an issuer that is not a competent authority or designated entity.

title.en: Determine which A1 pilots need the online exam and which need familiarisation only

description.en: UAS.OPEN.020(4) asks every A1 pilot to be familiar with the manufacturer's instructions, and adds the online training course and online theoretical examination only for pilots flying a class C1. A pilot flying a C0 or a sub-250 g aircraft needs no exam and, under UAS.OPEN.060(1)(a), carries no proof. Mark each A1 pilot with what the aircraft they fly requires.

evidenceHint.en: A1 roster extract marking each pilot's aircraft classes and the competency each requires

text.en: List the A1 pilots and the aircraft classes each flies.
Mark pilots who fly a C1 as needing the online training and exam.
Mark pilots who fly only C0 or sub-250 g aircraft as needing familiarisation only.
Note that the C0 and sub-250 g pilots carry no proof of competency.
Date the extract and update it when a pilot's aircraft change.

title.en: Train each A1 pilot on the manufacturer's instructions for every model they fly

description.en: The manufacturer's instructions carry the limits a pilot must fly within: weather, payloads, lost-link behaviour, how to load remote ID and zone data. Walk each A1 pilot through the instructions for every model they fly, including a practical run of its key functions, and record it before their first flight on that model.

evidenceHint.en: Familiarisation record per pilot and model with topics covered, date and trainer

text.en: Give the pilot the manufacturer's instructions for the model.
Cover the limitations, warnings and abnormal procedures they contain.
Practise the model's return-to-home and lost-link behaviour on the ground or in a safe area.
Record the familiarisation with the model, date and trainer.
Repeat it when the manufacturer issues a significant update to the instructions.

title.en: Obtain the A1/A3 online proof for each pilot who will fly a C1 in A1

description.en: A C1 pilot must complete the online training course and pass the online theoretical examination of the competent authority or its designated entity: 40 multiple-choice questions, at least 75%, across air safety, airspace restrictions, aviation regulation, human performance, operational procedures, UAS general knowledge, privacy and data protection, insurance and security. Have the pilot complete it before their first C1 flight and file the proof.

evidenceHint.en: A1/A3 proof of completion per C1 pilot with its identification number, issuer and date

text.en: Point the pilot to the competent authority's online course and exam.
Have the pilot complete the course and pass the exam before flying a C1.
File a copy of the proof with its identification number and issuer.
Record the issue date on the roster so validity can be tracked.
Allow C1 assignments only once the proof is filed.

title.en: Check C1 pilots carry their A1/A3 proof on every A1 flight

description.en: UAS.OPEN.060(1)(a) requires the pilot of a C1 to carry proof of competency while operating. Add a line to the C1 pre-flight checklist asking the pilot to confirm they carry the proof, on paper or electronically, and record it in the flight log.

evidenceHint.en: C1 flight log entries confirming the A1/A3 proof was carried

text.en: Add a proof-carried item to the A1 pre-flight checklist for C1 aircraft.
Confirm the proof is on the pilot's phone or in the kit before take-off.
Do not fly a C1 if the proof cannot be shown.
Record that the proof was carried in the flight log.
Report a lost proof to the training lead the same day.

title.en: Review A1 pilot competency records against flights flown each quarter

description.en: Each quarter, take the A1 flights flown and check every pilot was familiarised with the model they flew, every C1 pilot held a valid proof and carried it, and no C1 was assigned to a pilot without one. Raise findings and correct rostering.

evidenceHint.en: Quarterly A1 competency review sheet listing flights sampled, gaps found and findings raised

text.en: Select a sample of A1 flights from the quarter across pilots and models.
Check each pilot's familiarisation record for the model flown.
Check each C1 pilot's proof was valid on the flight date and carried.
Search rostering for C1 assignments to pilots without a proof.
Raise findings and correct rostering where gaps are found.

templates.title: Horizontal distance from uninvolved persons in subcategory A2
templates.description: In subcategory A2 the aircraft never overflies uninvolved people and stays at least 30 m from them horizontally, closing to 5 m only in low-speed mode after the pilot has weighed the weather, the aircraft's performance and how well the area is segregated.
templates.objective: To ensure every A2 flight keeps the distance from uninvolved people the regulation sets, and that each use of the 5 m low-speed allowance rests on a recorded evaluation.
templates.successCriteria:
No A2 flight log, track or incident record shows an overflight of an uninvolved person.
Every A2 flight plan states the horizontal distance kept from uninvolved people, measured from the aircraft's vertical-fall point and never less than its height.
Every flight that went below 30 m had low-speed mode active and a dated evaluation of weather, aircraft performance and area segregation made before it closed in.
Pilots stop or move away when an uninvolved person comes inside the planned distance, and the flight log records it.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the A2 flight plans, flight logs and telemetry or track exports for the period, with the operator's procedure for keeping distance from uninvolved people.
Obtain the record of every 5 m low-speed evaluation made in the period.
Obtain incident and occurrence reports that involve people near an A2 operation.

Analysis:
Sample A2 flights and compare the planned distance with the procedure: at least 30 m, at least the planned height, measured from the vertical-fall point.
For each sampled flight that went closer than 30 m, confirm the telemetry shows low-speed mode active at that time and that an evaluation covering weather, performance and segregation is dated before it.
Read the sampled tracks against the site plan for passes over areas where uninvolved people were present.
Compare the incident reports with the flight logs to find encounters the logs do not mention.

Output:
The proportion of sampled A2 flights whose plan and track meet the distance rule.
A list of sub-30 m segments flown without low-speed mode or without a prior evaluation.
Any overflight of an uninvolved person, with the flight, pilot and the action taken.

title.en: Define how A2 pilots measure and keep the distance from uninvolved people

description.en: Write the A2 distance rule into the operator's procedures so every pilot applies it the same way: never fly over an uninvolved person, keep at least 30 m away horizontally, measure from the point where the aircraft would land if it fell straight down, and never closer than the height being flown. Say who counts as uninvolved and that anyone who has not been briefed and agreed to take part is uninvolved by default.

evidenceHint.en: Approved procedure section stating the 30 m, 1:1 and vertical-fall measurement rules and the definition of an uninvolved person, with its approval date

text.en: State that A2 flights never overfly uninvolved people, whatever the distance or speed.
Set the minimum horizontal distance at 30 m, measured from the aircraft's vertical-fall point.
Add that the distance is never less than the height flown, so a 50 m flight keeps 50 m away.
Define an uninvolved person as anyone not briefed and not explicitly agreed to take part.
Approve the procedure and record its version and approval date.

title.en: Build the 5 m low-speed evaluation into the A2 pre-flight checklist

description.en: The regulation lets an A2 pilot close to 5 m only with low-speed mode active and after evaluating the weather, the aircraft's performance and how well the overflown area is segregated. Add that evaluation to the pre-flight checklist as a decision with a record, so the allowance is used on purpose rather than drifted into, and so an auditor can see the reasoning for each use.

evidenceHint.en: Pre-flight checklist with a 5 m evaluation block covering weather, aircraft performance, area segregation and low-speed mode, and the pilot's sign-off

text.en: Add a checklist block that is completed only when a flight will come closer than 30 m.
Ask for the wind, gusts and visibility on site and whether they are within the aircraft's limits.
Ask how the area is segregated, such as barriers, marshals or a closed site, and how well it holds.
Require the pilot to confirm low-speed mode is active and limits ground speed to 3 m/s.
Make the pilot sign and time the evaluation before closing inside 30 m.

title.en: Record the planned distance and any low-speed segment in each A2 flight log

description.en: For every A2 flight, log the horizontal distance planned from uninvolved people, whether the 5 m allowance was used and when, and anything that forced the pilot to stop or move away. Attach the track or telemetry export where the aircraft produces one, so the log can be checked against what was actually flown.

evidenceHint.en: A2 flight log entries with planned distance, low-speed segments and interruptions, plus the matching track or telemetry export

text.en: Enter the planned horizontal distance from uninvolved people before take-off.
Note the start and end time of every segment flown in low-speed mode below 30 m.
Record each time an uninvolved person came inside the planned distance and what you did.
Export the flight track or telemetry and attach it to the log entry.

title.en: Exercise the response when an uninvolved person walks inside the A2 distance

description.en: People wander into work sites. Run a short drill with each A2 pilot in which a helper plays a passer-by entering the planned distance, and check that the pilot reacts at once by stopping, climbing away or moving the aircraft so the distance is restored, rather than finishing the shot first. Record who took part and what the drill found.

evidenceHint.en: Drill record naming the pilots, the scenario played and each pilot's response time and action

text.en: Brief a helper to enter the planned distance at an unannounced moment during a training flight.
Observe whether the pilot stops or moves the aircraft away before the distance is lost.
Time the reaction and note whether the pilot told the observer what was happening.
Debrief the pilot and record any change to technique or procedure the drill shows.

title.en: Sample A2 flight tracks against the distance rule each month
